item.content:encoded:
A new study from Australia concludes that gay men might benefit from using more than one type of dating app. The results appear in Psychology & Sexuality.
“There are several fundamental differences between gay and mainstream dating apps that may significantly impact user experience, including the interface, image-sharing, and potential for non-consensual messaging,” says lead author Zac Bowman, a PhD candidate at Flinders University’s College of Human Sciences and Culture.
For example, on Grindr, you’re confronted with a wall of profiles that often feature plenty of flesh on display. You can exchange messages with anyone and may receive unsolicited, spicy photos. Previous studies have found that body objectification is rife on gay dating apps.
How about we take this to the next level?
Subscribe to our newsletter for a refreshing cocktail (or mocktail) of LGBTQ+ entertainment and pop culture, served up with a side of eye-candy.
By contrast, on Tinder and Hinge, you see users one at a time and swipe to indicate your interest. Messaging takes place only when users match.
The authors note that “Gay dating apps are used by an array of sexualities, including bisexual men, sexually curious men, or straight men looking for friendships”.
For this reason, their study sought the opinions of men from across the spectrum. They recruited participants via social media and Grindr adverts. In total, just under 580 men took part.
The researchers quizzed them on their app use and about their wellbeing. This included questions about body dissatisfaction, depression, anxiety, stress, and self-esteem.
What did the study find?
One of the study’s main findings was that queer users of both types of dating apps “reported significantly lower depression, anxiety, and stress scores than men who had used either mainstream or gay dating apps exclusively.”
By contrast, men who identified as straight reported more anxiety if they used both gay and mainstream dating apps. The authors speculate that the “straight” men who use gay dating apps might actually be struggling with their own sexuality, or fearful of judgement. Hence their greater anxiety.
“In contrast, for sexual minority men, participants who reported using both types of dating apps had significantly lower anxious symptomology than sexual minority men who used either mainstream or gay dating apps exclusively,” they say. “This result is surprising, as it not only opposes most previous literature reporting negative associations between dating app use and mental health, but also directly contradicts the relationship between using both app types and anxiety seen in straight men within this study.”
Why a diverse range of apps lessens anxiety in gay men
Why might using more than one type of dating app be better for your mental health? The authors suggest it might foster a feeling of having different irons in different fires, or maximising the chances of success, whether that’s seeking a hookup on a gay dating app or romance via a more mainstream app.
They say queer men “may have a wide range of motivations to access dating apps (e.g. love, sex, sexual identity exploration), and the use of multiple types of dating apps may increase the likelihood of achieving these goals.
“Perceived dating app success (i.e. achieving desired outcomes) has shown significant correlation with increased psychological wellbeing, and may therefore be a reason for the lower mental health concerns in sexual minority men who used both gay and mainstream dating apps.”
In short, the impact of dating apps on mental health isn’t one-size-fits-all — it depends on both the type of app and your orientation. Using a mix of platforms seemed helpful for gay guys but more complicated for straight men.

Overview
These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.
Table of Contents
If you've grabbed drinks with any single friend lately or scrolled through TikTok, you know the general consensus: dating apps are exhausting. App fatigue is very real, and it makes finding a genuine connection online feel like a second full-time job. As someone who's been testing and reviewing dating apps for years, I get asked one question over and over: Which dating apps actually work?
My answer is always the same: The only real "hack" is choosing the right app for what you actually want. Someone choosing eharmony may want a structured, relationship-focused experience, while someone on Tinder might be looking for anything from a casual hookup to a long-term partner. The important thing is finding an app (and people) whose goals line up with yours.
“It’s very common to spend days, weeks, or even months messaging with someone, become infatuated with the fantasy of them, and then get together in person and be disappointed,” Suzannah Weiss, sex/couples therapist and resident sexologist for Erojoy, tells Mashable. “I wouldn’t let more than a few days go by before transitioning to an in-person meeting or at least a video call.”

The best hookup apps, reviewed by our experts


AdultFriendFinder
—
readers’ pick for casual connections




Tinder
—
top pick for fast hookups




Hinge
—
popular choice for regular meetups




Pure
—
best for anonymous hookups




OkCupid
—
best app for inclusivity



So, before you delete your profiles and swear off romance forever, take a breath. Despite the burnout, people are still finding partners online. A 2026 SSRS Opinion Panel Omnibus found that half of U.S. adults who have used a dating site or app have been in a committed relationship with someone they met through one.
You just need the right tool. That's why I swiped, matched, and messaged my way through dozens of platforms to find the best dating apps of 2026. Whether you're looking for a serious commitment or just a casual weekend fling, these are the apps I think are worth downloading this year.
If you need even more personalized advice, check out our guides to the best dating apps for men, women, and gay and bisexual men.
The Good & The Bad
- Creative prompts and detailed profiles encourage more thoughtful connections
- You can attach a comment to a like and chat with matches for free
- Tons of ways to express yourself, including voice prompts and polls
- Inclusive platform with a variety of gender and sexuality options
- “Hidden Words” lets you filter unwanted words, phrases, and emoji from comments attached to incoming likes
- The free version limits your daily likes; unlimited likes require Hinge+ or HingeX
- The emphasis on prompts can sometimes feel like you're filling out a job application
- Filters for politics, dating intentions, and family plans require a paid subscription
Our review
Who it's for
Hinge is for daters in their 20s and 30s who are over swipe culture and want a real, meaningful relationship. It's the app I recommend to friends when they're ready to get serious and stop wasting time.
Why we picked Hinge
I picked Hinge as the best dating app overall because its "Designed to be deleted" slogan isn't just marketing. Instead of just swiping on photos, you can like a specific photo or prompt answer (like "My simple pleasures") and add a comment. You don't have to write anything, but making the first move about something on their profile gives you a better starting point than just "hey."
“Comment on something in the person’s profile, like an activity they’re doing in their photos or an interest listed in their bio,” Weiss says. “This will make your message stand out amid the generic ones.”
Hinge has also been rolling out useful, non-gimmicky features to help with the parts of dating people tend to overthink. The AI "Prompt Feedback" tool gives you advice on your prompt responses without writing them for you. Prompt Feedback is optional and private, so you can ignore the advice if your answer already sounds like you.
"Match Note” lets you share something privately with new matches before chatting, while “Convo Starters” gives you ideas for an opener based on their profile. (Again, you still have to write the message yourself.)
If the problem is figuring out what to share in the first place, Hinge also has a collection of 10 profile prompts developed with psychotherapist Esther Perel. Called "Your World," it includes prompts like "I'm in my element when..." and "I could stay up all night talking about..."
To help you get offline faster, Hinge offers "Date Ideas," a feature that lets you add up to three date ideas to your profile. Potential matches can pick one and select a window of availability, like "this weekend," from a drop-down menu. It doesn't schedule the date for you, but it helps you show you're both interested in meeting — and what you'd want to do.
Hinge's safety and security features
Hinge uses a mix of machine learning and human moderators to enforce its "ACE" (Authenticity, Courage, and Empathy) values. "Are You Sure?" nudges you before you send potentially harmful language, and "Hidden Words" lets you filter unwanted words and emoji in comments attached to incoming likes.
In October, Hinge also introduced an educational walkthrough for some minor harassment violations in chats. Human moderators assess the context and severity; users who receive a warning have to complete the walkthrough before continuing to use the app. Severe or repeated violations can still get someone banned. The idea is to teach better messaging etiquette rather than immediately remove everyone who crosses a line — not to give everyone a free pass for harassment.
Hinge's verification requirements vary by region; its age-check guidance explains what applies where you live. Regardless of the verification method, a badge isn't a background check.
Details
Details
The Good & The Bad
- You can browse profiles before committing to a paid subscription
- Free, unlimited messaging with mutual matches
- Detailed profiles include topics and interests that help you find conversation starters
- Free members get a daily intro to reach out beyond their mutual matches
- Seeing who’s already liked you requires a paid subscription
- The detailed profile setup can feel more time-consuming than swipe-first apps
- Multi-month subscriptions can mean a significant upfront commitment
- Unlimited likes and additional discovery tools require a paid plan
Our review
Who it's for
If you’re at a point in your life where you're over the games and just want to find a real, serious partner, I'd send you to Match. It's my go-to for daters in their 30s, 40s, and 50s who are established, know what they want, and are genuinely ready to find someone.
Why we picked Match
While the younger crowd is busy swiping on Tinder and Hinge, Match has carved out its niche as an option for a more mature demographic. The 2026 SSRS Opinion Panel Omnibus found that 33 percent of U.S. adults aged 50 and older who have ever used a dating site or app have tried Match.
In my experience, this means the crowd on Match is generally more invested (both emotionally and financially) in finding a real connection. That doesn't mean everyone is looking for marriage, or that having a subscription makes someone a better prospect. But if you're tired of trying to figure out whether someone wants a relationship at all, Match is one of the places I'd start.
The profiles give you room to explain your interests, lifestyle, and what you're looking for in a partner. That extra context is useful when you're trying to work out whether someone fits into your everyday life — not just whether you'd swipe right on their photo.
Match's safety and security features
Match offers anonymous reporting and says its team reviews every issue members report. You can report a concern from someone's profile or a message, including harassment, requests for money, or inappropriate behavior during or after an in-person meeting. Its reporting process is anonymous, and they've partnered with RAINN (the nation's largest anti-sexual violence organization) to improve their reporting, safety, and messaging features.
Match also warns against sending money to someone you've only met online — even if you've spent weeks talking and their emergency sounds convincing. Its safety guidance flags pressure to move off the app without meeting or video calling as another reason to be cautious.
Details
The Good & The Bad
- Inclusive gender and orientation options, with over 60 ways to identify
- Lets you be upfront about your dating goals, from casual hookups to long-term relationships and non-monogamy
- In-depth questions and compatibility scores help you compare values and preferences
- Quirky, text-focused profiles give you more to work with when starting a conversation
- Available on desktop as well as mobile
- Seeing everyone who’s liked you requires a paid subscription
- Answering lots of compatibility questions can make setup feel time-consuming
- Compatibility scores aren’t a guarantee of chemistry
Our review
Who it's for
OkCupid (also part of the Match Group) is my top pick for the open-minded dater who wants a feature-rich experience without having to shell out cash. It's one of the most inclusive apps out there, with over 60 ways to identify across its gender and orientation options, so it's great for the LGBTQ community. But the experience doesn't always live up to the promise.
In this Reddit discussion, some users describe the app as a "disaster," complaining about suspected bots and "passport" profiles from thousands of miles away. Of course, these complaints aren't definitive proof of what you'll encounter on the app, but they're worth reading through.
Why we picked OkCupid
I picked OkCupid as the best app for daters with dealbreakers because it’s the gold standard for comparing what matters to you before starting a conversation. While Hinge is my favorite free app overall, OkCupid’s free version is pretty impressive.
Its matching system is built on an in-depth questionnaire. You answer questions on everything from your political views to your messy habits, and the app gives you a compatibility score for other users. It's a way to spot potential dealbreakers before you even say "hello."
And those dealbreakers aren't just about politics or whether someone wants kids. In February 2026, OkCupid launched "Love & Money," a series exploring how finances shape modern romance. Among the Gen Z and millennial daters it surveyed, 63 percent considered being open about money a green flag, while 68 percent said financial responsibility was sexier than generosity. Apparently, sticking to a budget has its appeal.
OkCupid's safety and security features
OkCupid's safety policy is built on one simple rule: "don't be a jerk." The app uses a combination of "Safe Message Filters" (automated tools) and trained human agents to scan interactions and enforce its guidelines. Its rules prohibit nudity, pornography, and sexually explicit profiles, including kink/fetish profiles or descriptions of specific sex acts. If you're looking for a kink-positive space, I’d recommend Pure or Feeld, which has a "Reflections" quiz to help users explore their interests and desires.
The company also bans all photos of minors, including photos of yourself as a child. OkCupid also protects its inclusive environment by banning users for hate speech and for maliciously reporting other users (for example, reporting a trans person just for being trans).
However, you need to be cautious about the personal data you upload (as with any app, ever). In March 2026, the FTC announced a proposed settlement with OkCupid's operator and Match Group Americas over allegations that OkCupid broke its privacy promises by sharing nearly 3 million user photos, along with location and other information, with a third party. The allegations concern data sharing that began in 2014, not a new 2026 breach. The proposed settlement prohibits misrepresentations about data handling and privacy controls. It's a not-so-fun reminder of the data risks involved with dating apps.
Details
The Good & The Bad
- Widely available, with a presence in 190 countries — useful when traveling or exploring a new city
- Simple swipe-to-like interface makes it easy to get started
- Matching and chatting are free when you both like each other
- Relationship Goals lets people display what kind of connection they’re looking for
- Paid Passport mode lets you browse and match in another city before you arrive
- The free version limits likes and includes ads
- The photo-first swipe format can make it easy to judge profiles before considering compatibility
- Seeing who’s already liked you requires Tinder Gold or Platinum
- You generally need a mutual match before you can start a conversation
Our review
Who it's for
Tinder is the OG swiping app, and its main advantage is its massive user base. I recommend it if you're looking for casual dating, a quick hookup, or just to see who's out there. The vibe is focused on fun, not forever. While finding a serious relationship isn't impossible (Mashable's tech editor met his long-term partner on it), that's not what I'd download it for first. If you're looking for a hookup, Tinder is still the default.
Why we picked Tinder
I picked Tinder because its "swipe right" formula is a straightforward way to find a quick connection. But the big story is that Tinder is desperately trying to be more than just a hookup app. They've been adding Hinge-style prompts and an "Explore" page to help you filter for what you want, like "Serious Dater" or "New Friends." There's even a "Modes" feature that lets you switch into dedicated spaces, like "Double Date Mode" or "College Mode."
In September 2026, Tinder took the friend-group approach further with Group Hangouts, which launched in the U.S. and select markets. One person creates a group, picks an activity, and invites at least two friends. Once you have three members, you can browse other groups, match, and chat about meeting up. Everyone needs their own Tinder profile, so this isn't one person playing matchmaker from a shared account. If a one-on-one first date sounds exhausting, bringing your friends is at least a different way to start.
This year, the app is also using AI to tackle "swipe fatigue." Its "Chemistry" feature uses questions and optional Camera Roll analysis to suggest a small selection of profiles each day. Tinder announced its U.S. and Canadian rollout in March, following tests in Australia and New Zealand. Giving an app access to your photos isn't everyone's idea of romance, but that part is optional.
They’ve also added "Astrology Mode," which gives you quick insights into how you and a potential match vibe based on your signs, and revamped "Music Mode" to prioritize people with shared musical tastes. To get you offline, Tinder's "Events" feature lets eligible users discover local activities and see who's interested. It started in Los Angeles and expanded to additional major cities in July 2026, though availability still depends on where you live.
Tinder's safety and security features
Tinder's "Face Check" video selfie verification is designed to check that you're a real person and look like your profile photos. Availability and requirements vary by location.
But verification isn't foolproof. After reports showed scammers gaming the system, Tinder said it had updated its verification badging logic to look for greater consistency across profile images and review cases that needed more scrutiny.
The "Are You Sure?" and "Does This Bother You?" tools are designed to flag potentially harmful messages. Tinder announced AI upgrades in March 2026, including better detection before sending and automatic blurring of potentially disrespectful messages.
Details
The Good & The Bad
- Browse, match, and chat for free, with up to 100 likes per day
- Optional prompts and interest tags let you build a detailed profile without a lengthy mandatory questionnaire
- Dating intentions cover everything from a committed relationship to a physical connection
- The daily “Roulette” wheel lets you earn perks like boosts and rollbacks
- Consent Guard screens for explicit messages and images so you can decide whether to view them
- The distance filter controls who you see, not who can find and like your profile
- The free version includes ads, and the paid tiers and individual feature purchases can be confusing
- Revealing blurred likes requires an “Unblur” or paid access
- I found few women during my month of testing, despite setting my preferences to include them
Our review
Who it's for
Hily (short for "Hey, I Like You") is for anyone who’s exhausted the Tinder-Bumble-Hinge rotation but still wants to browse, match, and chat without paying. It's like a weird, morphed lovechild of Tinder and Hinge: You can fill out the basics and get going, or spend more time on prompts, interests, and what you’re looking for. Dating intentions include “Committed relationship,” “Something casual,” and “Physical connection,” so it isn’t exclusively a relationship app or a hookup app.
Your local crowd will make a difference, though. During my month of testing in a North Carolina beach town, I saw lots of outdoorsy, blue-collar men, many with conservative politics listed on their profiles. Think beards, fish pics, and very little ambiguity about what they wanted. I found far fewer women, even with my preferences set to include them. (That’s just based on my experience in one area, but I’d try HER first if you're looking for other queer women.)
Why we picked Hily
I picked Hily because its free version lets you browse profiles, send up to 100 likes a day, match, and have conversations without upgrading. You’ll see ads, and there are plenty of paid extras, but chatting with a mutual match is totally free.
There’s also more room for personality than the swipe-first format initially suggests. You can list up to 12 passions and answer prompts in categories like “My Dating Guide” and “Life Vibes.” If you want to dig further, the paid features include a 40-question “Icks & Clicks” Compatibility Check that highlights where your answers line up with someone else’s.
The daily “Roulette” wheel adds a little game-show energy by handing out perks like profile boosts and rollbacks. I appreciated that I could stop it from appearing at startup, too. Less charming is figuring out the difference between Premium, Premium+, and individual purchases like “Unblurs.” My advice: Start free and see whether you like the people before paying to get more visibility or reveal incoming likes.
One quirk worth mentioning: Your distance filter only controls the profiles you see in Finder. Someone farther away can still find and like you if their own search settings include your location. That explains why my "Likes" tab included people in other states even when I was trying to date locally.
Hily's safety and security features
Hily’s standout tool is "Consent Guard," which uses AI to flag potentially explicit messages and images and asks for your consent before showing them. It’s a useful layer of control if you’re open to flirting but don’t want someone else deciding when the conversation turns sexual.
The app also offers optional photo verification and a filter for verified profiles. A verification badge isn’t a background check or a guarantee that someone is trustworthy, so I’d still use the built-in video calling to get a better sense of a match before meeting. You can do that without exchanging phone numbers, and block or report someone from their profile if they make you uncomfortable.
Details
The Good & The Bad
- Sex-positive personal ads let you be upfront about your desires and dating goals
- Your real name and email aren’t displayed to other members
- Minimalist, artistic design stands out from other dating apps
- Built-in video calls, optional photo verification, and “True Photo” requests help you check who you’re talking to before meeting
- Media controls let you blur or block explicit photos in chats
- Photos are optional, and profiles can omit identifying details, leaving you with less information before starting a conversation
- Chats expire after 24 hours unless both people agree to turn off the timer
- Some privacy and visibility tools, including Incognito mode, involve paid features or subscriptions
- Disappearing photos and screenshot restrictions can’t prevent someone from recording your content with another device
Our review
Who it's for
Pure is for the adventurous dater who is so over the mainstream options and the endless stream of "heys" on other platforms. If you value anonymity, witty conversations, and getting straight to the point, this app is a breath of fresh air. It's designed for people who are tired of small talk and want to connect based on their unfiltered desires (which, ironically, you can filter for in the app).
The concept is clearly resonating. In February 2026, Pure reported $100 million in annual gross revenue and a 95 percent year-over-year jump in registrations at the end of 2025.
Why we picked Pure
After testing it for a month, my verdict is that Pure is "hot, weird, and way better than Bumble" for finding a connection. The app never asks for your name, and chats expire after 24 hours unless you both agree to turn off the timer. This creates a space for bold, honest conversations that I found were leagues above what I've experienced on other apps.
Instead of a long bio, you can post a short 350-character "personal ad" and customize it with the app's "Profile Aesthetics" and color patterns. Your "turn-ons" are front and center, and a "Mutual Turn-Ons" view instantly highlights exactly where your interests overlap with a match. Plus, the app is free for women, with an optional paid subscription called Pure Queen. It's an unconventional but surprisingly effective platform (especially if you're into steamy phone sex with strangers!).
Pure's safety and security features
Pure's entire platform is built for privacy. You don't have to put your real name on your profile, chats expire after 24 hours unless you both switch off the timer, and self-destructing photos and videos disappear after viewing. Pure says it blocks screenshots and alerts you to attempts, but someone can still photograph the screen with another device. You can also clear your chat history from both sides.
While anonymous profiles can be a red flag elsewhere, Pure balances them with clever safety features. You can also use the "True Photo" request to ask for a live photo in your chat and help check that the person looks like their photos. Pure also has My Media Rules, which lets you blur or block explicit photos, or block incoming photos and videos altogether.
In the UK, Pure has required age verification since July 2025. It starts with a face scan to estimate your age, with an ID and selfie check if additional confirmation is needed.
Details
The Good & The Bad
- Either person can start the conversation, so women don’t have to come up with every opener
- Private Detector blurs potentially explicit photos before you decide whether to open them
- In-app video and voice calls let you vibe-check a match without sharing your phone number
- Snooze Mode lets you take a break from new matches without deleting your profile or losing your existing conversations
- Matches still come with a deadline, which can make dating feel like another notification you need to deal with
- Profiles give you less to work with than Hinge if prompts and dealbreakers are your priority
- Seeing who likes you, advanced filters, and Incognito Mode require a Premium subscription
- The changing features and messaging rules make it harder to know what to expect from the app
Our review
Who it's for
I recommend Bumble for women and non-binary people who want a dating experience somewhere between the casualness of Tinder and the relationship focus of Hinge. That's still where it lands for me, even though the app has changed quite a bit since its "women message first" days.
Bumble now lets either person send the first message after matching. Once someone reaches out, the recipient has 72 hours to reply before the connection expires. So if you liked the idea of Bumble but hated being responsible for every opener, now's your chance to try it out.
Why we picked Bumble
Bumble's initial appeal was clear: it flipped the traditional dating script, putting the power to initiate contact in the hands of women and non-binary people. However, the app is currently in a state of flux.
The biggest change for everyday users is the updated chat experience. Either person can make the first move, but the conversation doesn't open until the other person responds. It isn't an invitation for anyone on the app to message you; you still have to match first.
The company is also testing "Dates," an AI-powered experience run by a personal dating assistant called "Bee." It starts with a private conversation about your values, relationship goals, communication style, and lifestyle, then recommends potential matches with an explanation of why you might get along. That's the pitch, anyway. I wouldn't treat an AI's explanation as proof that someone is your type.
That said, I'm keeping it on my list because it's still worth considering for its target audience (aka women who get shit done), but it's very much an app in transition.
Bumble's safety and security features
The old "women make the first move" rule is no longer the reason to recommend Bumble's safety features. Its more useful protections are the tools that help you control what reaches you and report something when it doesn't feel right.
Its best tool is the "Private Detector," an AI feature that automatically blurs potential nude images, so you can decide whether to open them or not. The app also uses an AI-powered "Deception Detector" to identify suspected spam, scam, and fake profiles, supported by human moderators.
Bumble also offers "ID Verification" (using a real government ID, not just a selfie) and a "Share Date" feature, which lets you send your date's info (like their name, time, and location) to a trusted friend.
Details
The Good & The Bad
- Built around long-term relationships
- In-depth Compatibility Quiz considers your values, personality, and relationship preferences
- Detailed profiles give you more to go on than photos
- Compatibility scores give you a starting point for comparing potential matches
- It's one of the more expensive dating sites on the market
- The free version is extremely limited: viewing unblurred photos and having unrestricted conversations require a paid subscription
- The Compatibility Quiz and profile setup take time
- You have less freedom to browse than on swipe-based apps, since the experience centers on recommended matches
Our review
Who it's for
If you're 100 percent focused on finding a life partner, eharmony is worth considering, though it wouldn't be my first recommendation for everyone. It's for daters who are ready to invest time in a thorough, data-driven process to find someone who shares their values. Its relationship-focused approach may appeal to older singles, but that doesn't mean everyone over 40 wants the same thing. The company's "Redefining Love After 40" report surveyed 3,016 U.S. singles in February 2026 and found that 56 percent said turning 40 gave them more time to focus on themselves.
Why we picked eharmony
To be blunt: I think you should try almost any of our other top-recommended apps before considering eharmony. When I tested it, the free version felt basically useless. You can explore profiles and send limited messages, but seeing unblurred photos and having unrestricted conversations requires a paid subscription. Plus, the mandatory Compatibility Quiz takes about 20 minutes.
That said, I'm keeping it on the list because for a very specific type of dater, the structured approach could be a good fit. If you have the budget, are ready for marriage, and want an algorithm to take the wheel, the questionnaire gives you more to work with than a few photos and a vague bio. The cost and setup may put off casual swipers, but neither guarantees that someone is genuinely invested. If you happen to be a "Charlotte York" type with disposable income, eharmony might be the best place to find your soulmate.
eharmony's safety and security features
eharmony has a dedicated Trust & Safety team and a community pledge built around being real, kind, and safe. That includes accurately representing yourself, treating other members respectfully, reporting suspicious behavior, and never sending money to someone you've met on the app.
Oddly enough, when I signed up, the app let me skip the photo upload step, which felt like a loophole for catfish on a platform this serious. That's another reason not to assume that a detailed profile or a paid subscription verifies someone's identity. You can report inappropriate behavior from within the app without sharing your personal contact details.
Details
The Good & The Bad
- A small batch of daily recommendations gives you a stopping point
- Preferences and previous likes and passes help shape recommendations
- Discover lets you browse beyond your daily suggestions
- Profiles and icebreaker questions give you conversation starters
- Daily recommendations can feel restrictive if you prefer browsing
- Discover offers additional browsing, but the experience is still more curated than swipe-first apps
Who it's for
I recommend Coffee Meets Bagel for people who are over swiping and want a more curated, less overwhelming experience. It often attracts young professionals in their late 20s and 30s who are looking for something more meaningful (it's like EliteSingles for the younger crowd). The app focuses on serious relationships, so it isn't where I'd send you for a casual hookup. Its own guidelines say CMB was designed to help people find long-term relationships.
Why we picked Coffee Meets Bagel
I picked Coffee Meets Bagel because its daily recommendations give you a stopping point instead of another endless feed. The matching process is pretty straightforward: you get a small, curated batch of "bagels" every day at noon. The app uses your preferences and previous likes and passes to suggest people, and you can browse additional profiles in Discover.
The coffee shop meetup is a low-pressure date idea, but CMB has been encouraging some daters to try a museum instead. In Singapore, the app launched a partnership with SG Culture Pass in February 2026 to push "cultural dates" (think galleries, workshops, and immersive exhibits) as an alternative to just another basic dinner. CMB's data found that 19 percent of women preferred concerts and live performances as date activities, compared with 9 percent of men. Museums and galleries appealed to 18 percent of women and 12 percent of men.
Its research also suggests that the young professionals using CMB have more practical concerns. In a November 2025 survey of about 1,050 U.S. users aged 21 to 35, 54 percent ranked financial stability as a top life priority. Nearly 60 percent named ambition or drive as a must-have in a partner. With rent and housing costs as they are, the app's leadership says young professionals are looking for ambitious partners who can help them afford a life together.
Coffee Meets Bagel's safety and security features
CMB has a zero-tolerance policy for hate speech, abusive behavior, and unsolicited sexual content. Its photo rules are extremely strict: At least one photo must clearly show your face, and all nudity, pornographic images, guns, graphic or gory images such as hunting photos, and AI-generated or deepfake images used to represent yourself are prohibited. And, like many of the other apps on this list, you can't upload photos of children by themselves.
The app is for dating, not soliciting, so it explicitly bans asking for money, linking to Venmo or PayPal, or sharing Amazon wish lists. The company also says it has a team working "around the clock" to find fakes and scammers, and all reporting is anonymous. Reporting someone automatically unmatches you, and CMB says it will follow up if its investigation leads to the account being frozen.
Details
The Good & The Bad
- It's built from the ground up for and by queer and gender-diverse people
- You can join the community, attend events, and find new connections for free
- Offers IRL and virtual community events, making it more than just a dating app
- Niche community tags (like "Newly Out" or "Polyamorous") let you find your people
- You'll need to pay extra to see who likes you
- Users report a noticeable number of unverified profiles and potential catfishes
- The experience is mobile-only; it's not available as a desktop dating site
Who it's for
If you're a queer woman looking for love, chances are you've had your fair share of frustrating experiences on heteronormative dating sites. Between straight people looking for threesomes and creepy men pretending to be women, finding a safe and inclusive space to meet potential partners can be tough. That's why I recommend HER, a dating app designed specifically for queer women, trans people, and non-binary individuals.
Why we picked HER
I picked HER because, as an app truly designed by and for queer women, it offers a refreshing and much-needed alternative to heteronormative platforms. To kick off 2026, the app published "The Sapphic Restart," a report on how its surveyed users were approaching dating. Among respondents, 67 percent cited healing, emotional depth, or entering a new life chapter as their main reason for restarting.
HER says it has over 15 million users worldwide, making it an option for queer women looking to expand their dating pool. I'm keeping it on my list because it's still the best in its class, but I'll be watching closely to see how the May 2025 Match Group acquisition affects the user experience over the long term.
HER's safety and security features
HER's rules are extremely clear and designed to protect the community. The app has no patience for TERFs ("Transphobes, you can kick rocks") and "chasers" (people who fetishize trans individuals). It also explicitly bans "unicorn hunting," so couples looking for a third to fulfil their fantasy aren't welcome to use HER for that purpose.
In the same Sapphic Restart survey, nearly 60 percent of respondents said their desire to date was rooted in wanting a secure, trustworthy connection rather than just excitement or physical touch. That's a finding about what respondents wanted, not a measure of how safe the app is.
A face photo is strictly required for safety and authenticity, and all nudes and photos of unaccompanied minors are banned. HER staff and community volunteer moderators can remove posts or profiles that violate the rules, though the guidelines acknowledge that moderators can't keep an eye on every comment or post. The app also provides dating safety advice, including having a voice or video call before meeting in person and using block or report tools if someone keeps pushing your boundaries.
Details
The Good & The Bad
- A large, established app for gay, bi, trans, and queer people
- You can message someone directly without waiting for a mutual match
- The nearby grid makes it easy to see who’s around instead of swiping through profiles one at a time
- Roam lets you temporarily place your profile in another city before a trip
- Free privacy tools include a discreet app icon, PIN protection, and the option to hide your displayed distance
- Be prepared to encounter unsolicited and explicit NSFW photos
- Many users report experiencing biphobia, transphobia, or racism on the app
- You’ll sift through profiles without clear face pictures or much information
- The free version is heavy on ads, and useful features sit behind a paywall
- Grindr Web requires an XTRA or Unlimited subscription
- Hiding your displayed distance doesn’t hide your position in the nearby grid
Our review
Read our recent reviews of Grindr and Grindr XTRA.
Who it's for
Grindr is the dating app for gay men. It also welcomes bi, trans, and non-binary people, though your experience will depend on who’s using it in your area. Keep in mind that Grindr is a very NSFW environment where many guys go to hook up. You might meet your soulmate, but that's generally not why people use it. And fair warning: modern-day Grindr is plastered with ads, and many beloved features are now behind a paywall, so you may want to consider upgrading to Grindr XTRA.
Why we picked Grindr
I picked Grindr because it's been the top gay dating app since 2009 for one simple reason: it's damn near-instantaneous. Instead of swiping, the app uses geolocation to show you a grid of nearby guys, which is especially useful if you're in a small town with a limited queer population. While the sheer number of users can be overwhelming, it also means there's a huge pool of men ready to chat.
Most users who are just looking to hook up will tell you that they're not trying to make small talk — and that warning may come in the form of a dick pic. That's not to say it's impossible to find a relationship (plenty of men meet their forever person on Grindr), but on the surface, it's a tool for quick, casual encounters.
Its “Right Now” feature also has a "Map View," which, if you opt in, shows participating users on a live map. (Availability is limited to select cities.) Your location is approximate, and you can adjust the offset or turn map visibility off. That gives you some control, but I wouldn't treat approximate location sharing as risk-free. You can adjust your filter to look for "dates," but don't be surprised when your options shrink dramatically.
If you have a lot of cash to burn, the app is also piloting an ultra-premium tier called "EDGE" in selected markets. It uses an AI stack called "gAI" to give you “A-List” summaries of conversations and missed connections, personalized profile recommendations, and profile insights. Test pricing varies, with reporting showing offers as high as $219.99 a week or $499.99 a month.
Grindr's safety and security features
Grindr offers privacy controls, but a discreet profile doesn't make you anonymous. You can hide your distance from the grid (though you'll still be sorted by location) and even change your phone's app icon to something discreet. The app also offers a PIN feature to lock the app.
Grindr's moderation team, which includes members of the LGBTQ+ community, uses a mix of automated tools and human review to enforce rules against harassment, hate speech, scams, and illegal activity. Depending on the violation, that can mean a warning, content removal, suspension, or ban.
Its Community Guidelines allow consensually shared nudity in private chats and albums, but prohibit sexually explicit public profile photos. That isn't permission to send unsolicited nudes: The rules specifically say to ask before sending explicit images or messages. You can send expiring photos in chats. You must be 18+ to use the app, or older where local requirements apply. Accounts suspected of belonging to someone under 18 are blocked and must complete ID verification to regain access.
Details
The dating apps I'd skip (and why)
You'll probably notice a few popular apps are missing from my list. That’s intentional. Part of my job is to filter out the platforms that aren't worth your time, money, or sanity. An app doesn't get my recommendation just because it's well-known — I need a good reason to send you there instead of somewhere else.
Here are a few popular dating apps I'd skip:
- Plenty of Fish (POF): I know this one shows up on a lot of lists, but it didn't make my cut. In my experience, sorting through suspicious and low-effort profiles made finding someone I actually wanted to talk to feel like more work than it was worth. Unless you enjoy doing that much filtering before you even get to a conversation, I think your time is better spent elsewhere.
- Raya: Raya is basically the Soho House of dating apps. It's exclusive, expensive, and not for the average person. You have to fill out an application and wait to see whether you're accepted through its vetting process. Getting in doesn't necessarily mean you'll have a better time finding a date, either. While it might be great for networking or bagging an influencer, it's just not a practical recommendation for most people who are simply looking for a date. (See also: The League.)
- Niche "hookup" sites (like BeNaughty, Fling, etc.): There's a chance you've seen ads for sites like these, which promise quick, no-strings-attached fun. That pitch alone isn't enough to earn my recommendation. I'd start with the hookup apps I've recommended instead, and read the subscription and cancellation terms carefully before signing up for any unfamiliar site.
Frequently Asked Questions
I've picked Hinge as the best overall dating app in 2026. Its "designed to be deleted" philosophy, creative prompts, and focus on detailed profiles make it my top pick for more thoughtful connections. But it's not the only app worth downloading. Tinder is still my top pick for casual hookups, and if you're looking for saucy, anonymous phone conversations, Pure is my favorite. If you've already tried the usual suspects, Hily is worth a look for its customizable profiles and mix of casual and relationship-minded daters.
In my experience, Match and eharmony are the best apps for daters over 40. I'd start with Match if you want to browse a more mature dating pool, or eharmony if you're specifically looking for a long-term commitment and don't mind a lengthy setup process.
My top pick for the best free dating app is Hinge. While OkCupid and Tinder also have robust free tiers, Hinge stands out because it allows you to send a comment with every "like" for free. That gives you a way to start a conversation about something on someone's profile instead of hoping a swipe does all the work. Hily is another good option: I could browse, match, and chat without upgrading during my testing. That said, if you're looking for something that's strictly casual and free, Tinder is your best bet.
For small towns, it's a numbers game. I'd start with Tinder, then compare the local options on Match and OkCupid. The best app is the one with people you'd actually want to meet within a distance you're willing to travel. A platform can be hugely popular nationally and still leave you scrolling through the same handful of profiles where you live.
My advice is to always try the free version first. If you like the app and think the premium features (like advanced filters or seeing who has already liked your profile) will genuinely save you time, then it might be worth it. The upgrade should solve a specific problem you're having — not just promise that your soulmate is hiding behind a paywall.
There's no dating app I'd call the safest across the board. Hinge and Bumble offer verification features, while Hily's Consent Guard requires consent before exchanging sexual messages or images. Those are useful protections, but a verification badge isn't a background check, and no app can guarantee that a match is trustworthy.
Tinder is the most widely used platform among U.S. online daters surveyed in the 2026 SSRS Opinion Panel Omnibus: 48 percent of adults who have ever used a dating site or app say they've used Tinder. That's a measure of past usage, not monthly active users. But as I always say, "most popular" doesn't always mean "best."
In my opinion, Hinge offers a better overall experience for most users right now. Its prompts and the option to comment on a specific part of someone's profile give you something to work with before you even match. Bumble is still worth trying, but if a friend asked me which one to download first for a relationship, I'd send them to Hinge.
Hinge is my overall recommendation, while Match is worth considering if you want a more mature dating pool. If you're marriage-serious, eharmony is another option. Its entire in-depth compatibility quiz is designed for singles who are all-in on finding a life partner. That doesn't make it a guaranteed shortcut to a relationship, but the structured approach may appeal to you if you're tired of swiping and hoping for the best.
Your profile is your personal ad, so make it a good one. Here are my top tips:
- Choose the right photos. Lead with a high-quality shot where you're smiling and look like your current self. Include a mix: a good headshot, a full-body shot, and pictures of you doing things you love. Resist the urge to overuse filters; authenticity is what people are looking for.
- Put some thought into your bio. Don't just say "I like food and travel." Get specific! "Trying to find the best ramen in the city" is a great conversation starter. A witty one-liner or a glimpse into your unique quirks can make all the difference.
- Use the prompts wisely. If the app has prompts (like Hinge) or matchmaking questions (like OkCupid), use them to show off your personality and goals.
Being safe is non-negotiable. Here are my rules for staying safe:
- Guard your personal info. Never put your full name, phone number, or home address on your public profile.
- Video chat first. A quick video call is a great way to vibe-check someone before meeting in person. If your dating app doesn’t offer calling, use a service that lets you connect without sharing your phone number.
- Meet in public. For a first date, always choose a public place like a coffee shop or restaurant.
- Tell a friend your plans. Let someone know who you're meeting, where you're going, and when you expect to be back.
- Trust your gut. If a conversation or person feels off, it's always okay to unmatch or block them.
Recommending a dating app isn't something I take lightly. Your time and money are on the line, and I'm dead serious about my mission to help you find a match. That's why my selection process goes way beyond just a few surface-level swipes. Here’s what my testing involves:
- Hands-on testing: I personally create profiles and spend weeks getting a feel for the user base on each platform. I use the free versions extensively, but I've also checked out the premium tiers to see what's worth the cost and what’s just a gimmick. I also look at whether newer features actually make it easier to find someone or just give you more buttons to tap before you get a date.
- Privacy and safety: I look into each app's privacy policies and safety features, like verification processes, moderation tools, and data sharing. This matters more than ever, given recent headlines about unauthorized data being used for AI training and massive security breaches. I track how these apps protect (or don't protect) your information and your person.
- Community and expert feedback: While I test every app on this list, my experience isn't the only one that matters. I also read Reddit threads and App Store reviews to see what the wider community is saying (and whether they're as annoyed by new AI bots as I am). I also consult other dating experts to make sure my recommendations are solid.
- Continuous monitoring: The app world changes fast (sometimes faster than your relationship status). I continuously monitor app performance, pricing changes, and new feature updates. This means I'm ready to update my recommendations if an app no longer lives up to its promise.
Tabitha Britt is an award-winning freelance journalist, editor, and SEO/AEO strategist. Aside from reviewing dating apps and sex toys for Mashable, Tabitha is also the founding editor-in-chief of DO YOU ENDO — a digital magazine by individuals with endometriosis, for individuals with endometriosis. She has a Master's degree in Creative Publishing and Critical Journalism from The New School for Social Research and is a grad of Sextech School. You can find more of her work in various online publications, including National Geographic, Glamour, Better Homes & Gardens, and Everyday Health.

item.content:encoded:
Sri Lanka Police have urged the public to exercise caution when forming relationships with strangers through dating apps and social media, warning of financial scams involving fraudulent mobile applications.
Several incidents have been reported recently in which scammers use dating apps to establish friendships or romantic relationships with victims, sending attractive messages over short or extended periods to gain their trust and deceive them.
According to police, scammers also approach individuals through social media and messaging platforms such as Facebook, WhatsApp and Telegram, claiming to offer online sexual services or opportunities to form personal relationships. Victims are then persuaded to download and install a specialised mobile application.
Police warned that these applications, which may appear to be dating apps, could be malicious APK files designed to compromise victims’ mobile phones and obtain their online banking credentials.
As a result, scammers may gain access to usernames and passwords associated with victims’ financial accounts when they carry out online transactions while the malicious application remains installed on their devices, enabling the fraudulent withdrawal of funds.
Police said methods used to commit financial fraud through social media and messaging platforms are rapidly evolving, with some scammers exploiting promises of love and companionship to deceive victims and gain access to their financial information.
The public has been urged not to install applications from unknown sources and to avoid sharing banking details, one-time passwords (OTPs), passwords or other personal information with strangers.
Police have also cautioned the public against sharing personal photographs or videos with unknown individuals.
Police stressed that making informed decisions when establishing online relationships is essential to protecting personal safety and financial security, urging the public to remain vigilant when interacting with strangers in the digital environment. (Newswire)

item.content:encoded:
You'd think that all these hyper-focused social media apps would make us more successful at reaching our goals, whether we're looking for love, connecting with friends, or trying to get a leg up in our career. But quite a few people are taking a more unconventional approach. Think using LinkedIn to find prospective dates—or swiping right for professional networking, not a hot date.
In fact, a recent Resume Builder survey found that one in three dating app users opted to use it for professional networking—including nearly half of those in the highest income brackets (earning $200,000 or more). And in the other direction, one in eight LinkedIn users have found romance on LinkedIn—even though 65% of those surveyed by Zety were concerned that it would damage their reputation.
So should you be seeking love (or a new job) in all the wrong places? Experts aren't so sure.
Stacie Haller, chief career advisor at Resume Builder
Kristen Zavo, career expert and author of Find Your Job Joy
Why People Are Shaking Up Social Media App Use
If you've been ghosted on dozens of job applications—or on dating apps—you can probably understand the appeal of trying something new to reach your goals.
"Traditional job-search methods can feel crowded and impersonal, and many job seekers struggle to get results," says Stacie Haller, chief career advisor at Resume Builder. "Candidates compete for attention on LinkedIn, while online applications often go unanswered, leaving people struggling to get noticed. Dating apps create a more natural setting for conversation, giving people the chance to establish a personal connection before professional goals enter the picture."
And people have been finding success with it—the Resume Builder research found that 88% of respondents who used dating apps for professional reasons successfully made a professional connection.
"Many job seekers are already familiar with these platforms, making them more comfortable reaching out to others and starting conversations—and that rapport can make networking feel less transactional and lead to genuine professional relationships," Haller says. "A conversation that starts around shared interests can lead to career advice, a referral, or an introduction to someone who can help open doors to new opportunities."
Why Experts Are Conflicted on Mixing Up Your App Game
Just because some people have found success with this unconventional approach doesn't mean it's a brilliant plan, and it can just as easily backfire on you.
"When we use a platform, there's an implicit understanding about why we're all there," says Kristen Zavo, career expert and author of Find Your Job Joy. "People are on LinkedIn to build professional relationships and explore career opportunities. They're on dating apps to find romantic connections. When someone approaches you with a completely different agenda, it can feel disingenuous and erode trust before a relationship even begins."
That can be especially true with reaching out for romance on a career website, which has been a major ick for many women. "I've personally experienced unsolicited romantic advances on LinkedIn, and I find them offputting," Zavo says. "Just because someone is accessible doesn't mean they're inviting every kind of interaction."
Bottom line: It's a risky move. "I'm all for creativity when it comes to building relationships and finding opportunities," Zavo says. "But there's a difference between thinking outside the box and approaching people with an ulterior motive."
How to Reach Your Goals the Right Way
Whether you're seeking personal or career fulfillment, there are ways to use this controversial approach in your favor—or find other methods that could be just as successful for you.
Be transparent about what you're doing
If you're using a social media account in an unexpected way, you need to be honest about that fact. "The key is transparency," Haller says. "Anyone using a dating app to make professional connections should be up front about their intentions rather than risk misleading someone. Not everyone on the app is looking to network, so it's important to respect those boundaries."
In either direction, it's a bad idea to start off in bad faith. "If someone is genuinely interested in getting to know you romantically, but you're primarily interested in accessing their professional network, you're starting the relationship on the wrong foot," Zavo says.
Be realistic about what you can achieve this way
Making a connection in an unexpected way may only get you so far. In job hunt terms, think of it more like an informational interview, where you may be able to add another point of contact that could get you closer to the job or relationship you want, rather than completely across the finish line.
"Expanding networking beyond traditional career platforms can help people connect with others who may play a role in their job search," Haller says. "Building relationships can help candidates get advice, secure referrals, and learn about roles they might not find on their own."
Shake up your job (or romance) hunt
If you aren't finding success with what you're doing, take a good hard look and see if there are ways to approach it differently, beyond reaching out on a different platform.
"When the job search starts to feel hopeless, the answer usually isn't sending out more applications, it's getting more intentional," Haller says. "Go after the roles you're genuinely a fit for, take the time to tailor your resume, and get your application in early. Most of all, talk to people. Someone who can vouch for you will get you further than a stack of cold applications ever will."
You may have better luck reaching out to people who are already in your network, Zavo says. "Rather than trying to turn a dating app into a job board, think about how you can expand your network in ways that create genuine connections. That might mean reconnecting with former colleagues, joining professional or community groups, attending events, or reaching out to people whose work genuinely interests you."
Take your hunt offline
We're all looking for a little (or a lot) less screen time, so put down the phone and mix and mingle toward your goal in a more expected setting—like an in-person speed dating get-together or a networking event, where you can more readily make the kinds of connections that you're seeking.
"Even as technology changes how people apply for jobs, personal connections remain an important part of how people get hired," Haller says.
"I absolutely encourage job seekers to prioritize relationship-building over simply submitting applications online, but there are much more authentic ways to do that than using a dating app as a networking tool," Zavo says. "My advice is simple: Be creative about how you meet people, but be genuine about why you're connecting with them. The best opportunities, whether personal or professional, often come from relationships we didn't initially expect—but those relationships need to be built on trust."

item.content:encoded:
The ‘non-toxic’ dating app that’s been built in Brunswick
Developer promises his app will deliver a ‘kinder and gentler’ dating experience
Does the world really need another dating app?
Alistair Kitchen thinks probably not – but it could do with a better one.
Fed up with the “enshittification” of popular apps like Hinge, Tinger and Bumble, the Brunswick writer has invented his own called One.
Touted as a kinder, gentler app, One has just been launched upon the world.
“The dating apps that are currently out there are causing a lot of pain and dissatisfaction in the world,” said Kitchen, who settled in Brunswick last year after returning from living in the United States for more than half-a-decade.
“They are, without exception, toxic, harmful, and extractive, and that’s because they’re all built on the same business model, and that business model causes these downstream effects, which incentivises the apps to keep people swiping, keep people alone, keep people single.
“I think the situation right now is dire, and we have an opportunity to replace these pretty toxic models with something a bit healthier, a bit less toxic, and a little bit kinder on single people.”
Kitchen says several aspects differentiate One from the other apps.
Most significantly, while it is currently free, users will eventually pay a one-off, lifetime fee to use the app rather than monthly subscription fees.
Kitchen promises that One will also provide a deeper, curated matchmaking experience based on a five to 10 minute verbal questionnaire to determine compatibility with potential matches.
And rather than swiping left or right based on a person’s brief profile and/or photo, One users will only be provided with three to five potential matches each day and will be restricted to choosing just one of them.
“The big difference is those apps are uncurated, and this app is heavily curated, so people can spend a lot less time swiping and a lot more time connecting,” Kitchen said.
Now 34, Kitchen has been a user of dating apps since Tinder arrived on the scene during his first year of university.
“I came of age and was thrown into this new world and, like I think a lot of people, found the dating apps in that era – 2012 through to, you know, 2018 – to be really additive and interesting and kind of vibrant,” he said.
“And then pretty soon after that they rapidly started to enshittify.”
‘Enshittification’ is a phrase coined by the Canadian writer Corey Doctorow to describe the process of how online and mobile products and services degrade over time as financial realities mean their developers are forced to compromise on their original principles.
“My personal experience was these incredibly useful, interesting, vibrant technologies degraded before my eyes,” Kitchen continued.
“And it got to a point where I thought, well, someone should build a business model which will not incentivise the apps to enshittify.”
One took about six months to build before a low key launch to a local inner northern suburbs market. It has gained about 500 users in its first few weeks in Apple’s and Google’s app stores.
After it reaches about 1000 users, Kitchen will broaden marketing of the app and introducing a price (probably $100), although he has no aspirations for global domination.
Kitchen’s name may be familiar as he was in the news last year after he was detained and refused entry to the United States because of what he alleged was his political activities.
Kitchen lived in the US for six years, including a period studying creative non-fiction writing at Columbia University in New York City.
According to reports at the time, Kitchen had been travelling from Melbourne to New York to visit friends when he was detained and interrogated for 12 hours at Los Angeles airport about blog posts he wrote on protests at Columbia University against the war in Gaza during his time as a student there.
But the US Department of Homeland Security said the reason why he was sent back to Australia was for giving false information on an entry form.
The incident gained attention because it was during the Trump government’s crackdown on immigration and dissent.
Kitchen has lived in Brunswick for about a year, choosing an apartment in the area because “it was the closest thing to my life in New York”.
Despite developing an app, he said he was first and foremost a writer and was working on a book of essays about gender and masculinity in Australia, which he had begun writing and researching while he was studying in the US.

item.content:encoded:
Dating apps aren’t delivering when it comes to finding a life partner.
Single people are getting sick of swiping and abandoning dating apps in droves. That’s left the apps themselves desperately attempting to pivot amidst public backlash against their business premise — to the point of turning their backs on what made them successful in the first place.
Tinder, which made billions on the idea that people want to meet one another easily online, has taken to hosting in-person events. Bumble, which just made a deal to go private after years of its stock price tanking, has turned its back on its feminist mission, which used to require women to make the first move.
They’re trying anything to keep public trust, despite the fact three-quarters of Americans now believe dating apps have made romance feel transactional, per a 2026 Harris poll.
“[The apps] took the friction out of finding someone, but they also took the friction out of exiting, which means that you weren’t getting the depth of the experience,” Boston University business professor Marshall Van Alstyne told The Post.
“Initially, they were creating a lot of value to get folks on board [lots of people to potentially date], but now they’ve entered the extractive phase [charging subscription fees], and I think we’re now seeing the consequences.”
Business is looking pretty grim. Match Group, which owns Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid, and many other platforms, laid off 13% of their workforce last year, and Bumble 30% last June.
Bumble once had 12.5 million users who spent an average of 100 minutes a day swiping, but the app’s paying users fell by almost 17% year-over-year, and revenue dropped 15% during the same period.
Since going public in 2021, Bumble has lost 90% of its market value. The struggling app made a deal last Tuesday to go private for $1.3 billion — chump change compared with its $14 billion valuation at its initial public offering.
To New York City matchmaker Maria Avgitidis, part of the problem was going public in the first place — shifting obligations away from hooking users up to line shareholder pockets: “[The apps] had to find the equilibrium between providing a good product and also providing positive returns to their shareholders. And sometimes those things are not going to align.”
When Bumble was founded in 2014, it positioned itself as a feminist alternative to Tinder, led by a female CEO who put women in control by requiring them to send a message to their matches first.
As of August, the app had turned its back on that fundamental premise, and now anyone can send the first message — making it virtually indistinguishable from competitors.
Even the female founder and CEO herself, Whitney Wolfe Herd, is stepping aside to make room for two incoming male CEOs upon going private. Bumble did not respond to request for comment.
Amy Andersen, the self-described matchmaker of Silicon Valley, believes the apps’ contraction is part of a larger disillusionment with the idea that romance could be made simpler by algorithms.
She told The Post she’s noticed a “huge exodus from the apps” that’s escalated in the last three years — even among the techies who literally founded them.
“I have had clients literally be the ones who have built the app, but they’re not using it when it comes to their own personal lives,” she said. “The machine professionally dominates their lives, yet when it comes to the intricacies of their personal lives, they’re choosing the human.”
Another app trying to reinvent itself is Tinder, which has seen monthly active users decline 7% year-over-year as of March and whose parent company Match Group is increasing Tinder’s marketing budget by $50 million this year.
After almost fifteen years in the business of matching people seamlessly online through a swipe, they’re moving into the events space and offering users in-person gatherings on a new tab in the app. Tinder told The Post that they’ve facilitated over 1,700 events so far and hope to reach 75 cities by the end of the year.
They seem to have reached an unlikely conclusion: that staying alive in the online dating space might require recreating the sort of social scenarios apps were originally aiming to replace.
Tinder has also tried to get people together in groups, rather than on one-on-one dates. They launched “double date mode” in 2025, and last month added group hangouts to their offerings. “We’re building ways to lower the pressure on Tinder,” a spokesperson told The Post.
“Ultimately, our goal is to make finding a spark feel more fun, authentic and connected to real life.”
The move comes as singles are flocking to more old school methods of finding partners. They’re joining running clubs and pickleball leagues in hopes of finding the one, and setting up their friends with potential matches. Meanwhile, in-person singles events hosted on Eventbrite literally doubled between 2022 and 2025.
Disillusioned singles are also trying out good old-fashioned matchmaking — tasking a human, rather than an algorithm, with finding them love. Chris Kumar, CEO of the country’s largest online matchmaking service Tawkify, said his platform has grown 30% year-over-year.
The upswing, he says, is part of a larger story of “dating app fatigue” and singles desperately looking for a more substantive alternative.
“The apps lost the elegance of what it means to be online and have that spark of connection with someone who swipes on you. That just isn’t exciting anymore,” he said. “So [the apps are trying] to find ways to reinvigorate that hope and that excitement from singles.”
The whole transformation seems to point to an uncomfortable conclusion: the future of dating apps may be one where the apps themselves take the back seat, and let singles find one another on their own terms. Its the clearest proof yet that Cupid’s mysterious ways can’t be distilled into an algorthim and true love remains as unpredictable and sometimes elusive as ever.

In the digital age, the dating scene has drastically changed; instead of meeting in bars or through mutual friends, many people meet their partners-to-be on dating apps.
This includes San Francisco-based dating coach Alan Chan, who said he spent about a year and a half on dating apps after a long-term relationship from the age of 20 to 26, until he met his fiancée on Tinder.
“I was very new to the dating app scene,” Chan said. “By the time I matched with my fiancée, I was so tired of it. I was like, ‘Let’s just go on dates and have fun.’”
A 2019 Pew Research Center poll found that three in 10 surveyed U.S. adults have used a dating site or app; although Chan recommended dating apps as a tool, he said people shouldn’t solely rely on them to find a partner.
“Dating apps are probably where you’re going to meet someone,” Chan said. “I would also recommend attending parties, … especially if you’re a full-time worker, which most of us are, it’s very hard to meet people.”
Since meeting his fiancée, Chan started coaching others in finding partners, including one client who found a girlfriend after two weeks.
“Every day you’re out is an opportunity to meet someone,” Chan said. “All it takes is eye contact, a smile and a conversation.”
Communications major Sophie Everett, 22, said they met their current partner of three years on Hinge; however, they said they wouldn’t push dating apps onto others just because of their good experience.
“I wasn’t looking for anything serious,” Everett said. “He (my partner) was kind of plopped into my lap.”
Everett also said they believe dating apps can be good in some ways.
“You can meet people (on dating apps) that you wouldn’t have met (otherwise),” Everett said.
Julia Le, 19, accounting and film production major, said dating apps aren’t for her.
“I definitely see the value in them,” Le said. “Personally, it just doesn’t work.”
Le said she hasn’t been on dating apps for a while and prefers meeting people organically, but has tried them before.
“I never had a serious relationship that came out of a dating app,” Le said. “People have really good experiences there, but the good experiences are few and narrow compared to the vast majority.”
A 2024 Computers in Human Behavior study found that people who meet on dating apps have less stable marriages.
Accounting major Larry Maciel, 20, said he thinks dating apps are horrible.
“People have unrealistic expectations whenever they go on one,” Maciel said. “They expect to find the love of their life or they think that the app is going to solve all their problems.”
A 2024 Pew Research Center study found that while U.S. adults’ perceptions on dating apps skew positive, only 10% of partnered adults met their current significant other through a dating site or app.
Pew’s survey also found that 24% of partnered lesbian, gay or bisexual adults and one in five partnered people under 30 met their partners on dating sites, a far higher rate than other demographics.
Despite his thoughts on dating apps, Maciel also said he has found cool people on them.
“It (a dating app or website) is an OK way to meet people, especially if you’re shy or have anxiety,” Maciel said. “Know what you’re getting into when you download it, and go in without any expectations.”
