item.content:encoded:
By Ben Barry
A relationship coach says dating apps are not to blame if you're single - and reveals her four tips to find love on them.
Sabrina Zahar, 36, is a dating and relationship coach with four years of experience in the field.
She believes that dating apps aren't inherently the problem with modern-day dating and argues that users' expectations and how we use them are to blame.
Sabrina compares dating apps to casinos, saying that the house is always going to win.
She says people need to be discerning, recognize that others are at different stages of life and take breaks when dating burnout sets in.
Sabrina also said that modern life has exposed humans to more rejection than ever before, and that the reason people stay single while using the app is because of their expectations and how they are using it.
Sabrina, from Los Angeles, California, said: "The way I look at apps is kind of like a casino.
"The house is always going to win, but do I blame the casino for people having a gambling problem?
"No, because that's an internal situation that people are coming into.
"Of course, are we at a time where it's a bigger, better deal? You can swipe and find new people, absolutely.
"But I also think that we have to hold space for the fact that we are getting rejected so much more than we ever have simply by having these phones, right?
"I think what I start to see is the issues people have with the dating app are more about their expectations and how they're using the apps than it actually being the apps."
Sabrina said she was on and off the dating apps from the age of 19 until she met her partner.
While she was on the apps, Sabrina said it was more about "who was good looking" and "who was picking me".
She said: "I have been on and off the dating apps most of my adult life.
"When I first used the apps, it was more just who's good-looking? Who's picking me? And things like that.
"It wasn't actually about anybody choosing me; it wasn't me choosing people. I was more bothered about people choosing me."
Sabrina admits she "slept my way through Manhattan" and realized that she needed to "reframe" her approach to dating apps.
First, she turned off all of her notifications on the apps and turned her focus onto men who were matching with her.
"I was in a dopamine-rewarded loop with the apps. I was constantly checking and checking them," Sabrina said.
"I realized that I need to reframe not only my expectations of apps and then how I used them.
"I turned all off the notifications off; I focused on people who were matching with me so that I could see if they were people I was interested in, so I didn't feel like I was constantly overperforming.
"I didn't chat with people for more than a couple of hours; I didn't get into texting loops with people.
"I was very intentional with the way I created my profile to showcase what I was looking for, and turning off the notification allowed me to create boundaries for how often I went on."
Sabrina said buzzwords like "red flag" and "attachment style" are harming dating culture.
She argued that people are too quick to label behaviors as narcissistic, avoidant or red flags, rather than recognizing the difference between personal preferences and genuine behavioral patterns.
Sabrina said the constant analyzing can lead to hypervigilance and fear, preventing people from trusting themselves and forming genuine connections.
She said: "We hear the word narcissist thrown around as if it's the word hello, right?
"Like red flags are patterns of behavior, not just something that you don't like or the fact that they didn't open the door for you. That's not a red flag. That might just be a preference for you.
"And I think so many people, you know, it's the same: we see the avoidant and the anxious, and people are trying so hard to consciously understand that they're not actually connecting anymore.
"They're playing detective, and they're hypervigilant, and all they're doing is looking, looking, looking and scanning for safety as opposed to actually being in connection and trusting themselves."
On Oct. 15, 2026, Sabrina launched her book "Why Am I Like This?".
Sabrina says her book combines psychology with personal experiences and hopes that readers will actively implement the lessons learned from the book.
Sabrina said: "Honestly, I was the girl that needed it. I was the hot mess, right? I slept my way through Manhattan, which is a very nice way of me saying I was finding myself, right? You said jump, I said on who.
"I was the girl that had so much anxiety and core beliefs and didn't believe in myself. And once I started to do this work and realized it.
"Now here's the harsh reality: a lot of the concepts in the book, they're not revolutionary because psychology hasn't changed that much.
"Humans are still humans, but what I've done is I've created a narrative and a story throughline with my own experience as well as the clients that I've worked with for the last four years to create a very clear, oh, that's how this works.
"So the first half is why, but then we go into now. What are you going to do with it? The book won't change your life if you just read it cover to cover in 24 hours and throw it back on your shelf.
"The book will change your life if you stop, you implement, you do the exercises, you start to get curious, you hold yourself accountable, you set the boundaries, you learn fundamentally about these concepts for yourself."
HER TIPS ON HOW TO FIND LOVE ON THE APPS:
- Turn off your notifications
- Only focus on people who are matching with you
- Don't get into a texting loop with someone - unmatch if they don't make plans
- Create your profile to reflect what you're looking for

Lez take a look at the dating lives of queer women and non-binary people
BY SOFIE ROOS, IMAGE BY DIVERSIFY LENS/CANVA
The modern dating world is fascinating. But what is it like for queer women and non-binary people? Let’s take a look at some interesting facts that shed some light on the realities of lesbian and sapphic dating.
For sapphics, love often begins with friendship
According to a 2022 article, as many as 85% of queer people said that their relationship began with friendship.This older study, found that friendship is the start of many lesbian relationships. It’s obvious that the line between being just friends and being something more is much thinner for sapphics!
Dating apps play a bigger role for queer women when dating
According to a 2023 article in Pew Research Center as many as 51% of American lesbian, gay and bisexual adults have at least once used a dating app, compared to 28% of straight people. It also shows that as many as 24% of queer people have met their partner online. While the research (unfortunately) doesn’t specify the exact sapphic number, it tells us that queer women are more likely than heterosexual women to look for love online.
Queer women aren’t exclusively looking for love or sex on the apps
A review of 21 studies published in 2022 found that dating apps serve more functions than just finding a sex or romantic partner for queer women. For some sapphics, dating apps are used just as much for finding new friends, building a community, or just to feel that there are others like you.
Sapphic dating can be pure detective work
The same research found that sapphic dating involves some detective work, because queer women tend to balance between visibility and privacy while dating. Sapphics want to say “Hey, I’m into women” to the right people, and at the same time. We can be careful about how much personal information we reveal. This means that sapphics have to invest more time into thinking, “Hmmm, is this person even into queer women?”.
Sofie Roos is a licensed sexologist and relationship therapist as well as author at the Swedish sex and relationship magazine Passionerad

item.content:encoded:
Black woman changed her race to white on Hinge and suddenly started matching with investors, advisors and athletes: ‘That racist’
Finding a good match on dating apps can be frustrating. But one Black woman claims her options improved almost overnight after she changed her race to white on Hinge. The difference left her questioning how the app was treating her.
Before the change, she struggled to find men she wanted to date. Suddenly, her feed was filled with Harvard graduates, investors, and athletes. Interestingly, some of those men were Black.
A video shared by TikTok account @wrekkkii, which has gained 28.6K views, captured the woman’s experiment. While she encouraged other Black women to try the same trick, commenters weren’t convinced. Some questioned whether those new options were actually any better.
Then came the questions
The woman explained that she had seen another person recommend the trick a few months earlier. The advice was for Black women to identify as white on dating apps to improve their dating options. Curious whether it would work, she decided to test it herself.
Her Hinge profile originally identified her as Black, although she had hidden that information from other users. According to her, the men appearing in her feed were mostly drug dealers, scammers, and people she had no interest in dating.
Then she changed her race to white, and the difference surprised her. “Suddenly I’m getting Harvard graduates, real estate investors, financial advisors, um, football players, black men,” she recalled.
She was particularly surprised by the attractive Black men appearing in her feed. “Where were y’all?” she asked, wondering why she hadn’t encountered those profiles before.
“Shit is that deep and that racist,” she wrote in the video’s caption, expressing her frustration with the difference in her dating options.
For the woman, the experiment raised questions about racial bias in online dating. She encouraged other Black women to try changing their race, arguing that dating apps weren’t taking them seriously.
However, commenters pointed out a potential problem with her advice. Even if the change made more desirable profiles appear, it didn’t necessarily mean those men would be interested in dating her.
Several people suggested that the men appearing in her feed might have set their preferences to exclude Black women. If that were the case, changing her race could make their profiles visible without changing their actual preferences.
“Why would you want men who are seeking white women?” one commenter asked. Another responded, “Those are men that don’t want you. Disregard them and move on.”
Others felt the experiment reflected broader dating challenges Black women face, particularly when racial preferences influence who gets considered as a potential partner.
“that’s because those men have clearly removed black women as their preferences and it’s time for black women to wake up and see it,” one person wrote.
Another pointed out that seeing someone on a dating app doesn’t guarantee romantic interest. “Those men selected to be shown white women so it probably won’t change your odds.”
One commenter raised safety concerns about appearing to men who may have deliberately excluded Black women. “My concern is if those men have their settings set to intentionally filter out black women, will changing those settings make your profile visible to some men who could be a threat to your safety,” they wrote.
Changing her race may have brought different men into her feed, but it doesn’t guarantee better dating prospects. After all, finding someone worth dating should depend on genuine compatibility, not having to pretend to be someone else.

item.content:encoded:
Be careful when swiping right, because there's a very good chance the other person could be a scammer.
Democratic Senator Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire and Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee released the results of their bipartisan congressional investigation into dating apps this week — and the findings are pretty shocking.
The investigation looked into romance scams on Match Group platforms, which include Tinder, Hinge, Match, Plenty of Fish and more. Per a press release from Hassan's office, views of scam profiles on Tinder alone increased by more than 700 percent between May 2024 and December 2025.
According to the committee's findings, Match Group "knew that Tinder was more likely to show a profile if it belonged to a scammer or other bad actor rather than a regular user." The report also says nearly 1.5 million scammers or bad actors on Tinder and Hinge matched with another user — and nearly 500,00 of those accounts exchanged contact information with others.
The scams usually involve fraudsters forming virtual relationships over the apps, asking their victims for money or gifts. They're now considered one of the leading forms of fraud in the U.S., with the Federal Trade Commission reporting nearly $1.5 billion in losses last year to romance scams — which Hassan's office says is a nearly 650% increase since 2019.
While Hassan said Match Group has "made progress in combating scammers," she added that it "shouldn't have taken so long" for action.
"There's still more that Match needs to do," she said in a statement.
Among those improvements is a new video verification process, Fact Check, on Tinder, which Match Group said has reduced user interactions with scammers by more than 70 percent. It was deployed nationwide back in December 2025.
After the committee's "continued" followups with Match Group about their outdated AI models, they also introduced a new model in early 2026 that is said to better detect fraudsters.
In a statement to NBC News, Match Group's senior vice president of trust and safety Yael Roth said the company "is grateful the Committee recognized our significant advancements to protect our users against romance scams."
"That said, the report mischaracterizes both the historical scale of our investment and the work already completed. Alongside our engagement with the Committee over the past year, we've made the largest safety advancements in Match Group's history," the statement continued. "Trust and Safety is a foundational priority, and we intend to continue leading the industry in building tools that promote authentic, safe connections."
In September, Congress passed the Romance Scam Prevention Act, which Hassan explained will require dating apps to notify people if they've interacted with any scammers who were later banned. President Donald Trump still needs to sign it into law.
Hassan also introduced the ReportScams.gov Act, which aims to create a "centralized portal where Americans can report scams and get help."

Why singletons are fall-ing in love in the autumn (and snubbing dating apps)
As the evenings begin to close in and the long, hot summer is consigned to memory, some of us may find ourselves contemplating another seasonal change.
There may even be a biological component. Testosterone levels in men fluctuate seasonally and tend to be higher during winter, potentially influencing the motivation to seek a sexual partner.
Despite all this talk of coupling up, however, Graff points out that the clue is in the word ‘season’. Cuffing traditionally refers to a temporary liaison during the winter months rather than the pursuit of a long-term relationship. So perhaps hold off on clearing him a drawer.
The figures from Your Friend, My Friend point towards the latter. Keating says 82% of attendees meet somebody they are attracted to at an event, while more than 70% have gone on a date afterwards. Increasingly, she says, people are treating singles events as a genuine alternative to apps rather than something to try once for the novelty.
Among Gen Z, however, she is seeing the opposite: Men are increasingly proactive and enthusiastic about attending, and men’s tickets are now selling faster than women’s. A speed dating event for ages 22-33 run by Your Friend, My Friend in Dublin this week tellingly had the sign ‘Men Sold Out’ up.

Welsh star makes candid dating app admission after filming new drama 'I've given up'
Welsh actress Elen Rhys has opened up about her love life, admitting she has “given up” on dating apps
Welsh actress Elen Rhys has made a candid admission about her own love life after revealing she has “given up” on dating apps.
The actress, who returns as detective Ffion Lloyd in the second series of hit Welsh crime drama Cleddau, opened up about her experience with online dating while discussing her character's own difficult encounters with the apps.
And while Ffion is still putting herself out there in the hope of finding love, Elen admitted she has decided to step away from dating apps in her personal life.
Asked whether she had ever had a bad experience using them, she said: “Oh, God, haven’t we all? I’m… I’ve given up on dating apps in my personal life.”
The subject takes on particular significance in the new series, with Ffion's attempts to move forward romantically becoming tangled up in one of the cases she is investigating.
In series two, Ffion is trying to rebuild her personal life and has started using a dating app. But when a woman's body is discovered in the River Cleddau, detectives begin to suspect that a killer could be using the same app to target victims.
Suddenly, something Ffion had been using as a way of finding companionship becomes part of a disturbing murder investigation. Elen said it was an interesting aspect of the character to explore because Ffion's dating life runs alongside the central investigation.
She said: “But what was really nice playing was… she is dating online. That runs parallel to this investigation.” The new series promises to take Ffion into much darker territory as her professional investigation begins to collide with her personal life.
Her complicated relationship with Rick, played by Richard Harrington, also remains unresolved. Rick is now separated and single, leaving the door open for the pair's relationship to develop as Ffion attempts to work out what she wants from her own life.
But the new case also forces Ffion to revisit a traumatic period from her past, adding another layer to an already complicated investigation.
As the pressure mounts, Ffion takes a personal risk which could have serious consequences for both the case and her career.
The first series of Cleddau became a major hit for S4C and attracted record numbers of iPlayer sessions for an S4C drama series.
Away from the drama, Elen has largely kept her private life away from the spotlight. She is a mum to her young son and has previously spoken about balancing motherhood with her demanding acting career.
The actress has built an impressive career across television and film, with roles in Keeping Faith, The Mallorca Files, Broadchurch and Silent Witness, as well as appearances on the big screen.
Series two of Cleddau launches on S4C and BBC iPlayer on October 11

St Mary man allegedly used dating apps to lure, rob women
ST MARY, Jamaica — A man accused of using dating applications to lure and rob women has been convicted on ammunition charges in the St Mary Parish Court, while 12 other criminal cases, including rape, robbery and firearm offences, remain pending against him.
Demoy Pennington, a 41-year-old bar operator from Gordon Hall, Epsom, St Mary, was the subject of an islandwide manhunt before his capture on June 24 in St Mary.
Pennington, who has previous convictions, including for grievous sexual assault, is accused of impersonating well-known personalities, including police officers, to deceive women he reportedly met through dating applications.
Investigating officer Dr Jason McKay revealed that Pennington was apprehended by a joint police team after investigators from the St Catherine South Police Division tracked him to St Mary.
“It’s one case down, 12 to go,” McKay said, referring to the outstanding criminal matters.
“He probably thought he was safe in St Mary but St Catherine South has gone as far as St Thomas in the east and Hanover in the west in pursuit of parish-hopping criminals,” he added.
Pennington’s arrest followed investigations into an alleged incident on June 3 involving a woman he reportedly met through a dating application.
According to police reports, Pennington picked up the woman in Kingston, and the two travelled towards Hellshire Beach in Portmore, St Catherine.
While travelling along Port Henderson Road, Pennington allegedly stopped at a business establishment and asked the woman to purchase a bottle of water.
The woman reportedly left her handbag, containing her mobile phone, bank card and other personal belongings, inside the vehicle. However, when she returned, Pennington and the vehicle were gone.
The matter was reported to the police, and subsequent investigations reportedly revealed that $7,000 had been withdrawn from the woman’s bank account using her card.
Pennington was later positively identified during an identification parade and charged with simple larceny and unauthorised access to computer data.
He had previously been charged in connection with at least two other incidents involving the alleged robbery of women he met through dating applications.

item.content:encoded:
A judge ruled Friday that a model and social media influencer accused of stealing from people she met through dating apps is mentally competent to stand trial.
Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Maria Cavalluzzi announced Friday that psychiatrist Dr. Phani Tumu found Adva Lavie, 29, “presently competent,” according to media reports. The finding clears the way for criminal proceedings to resume after they were suspended in August.
Lavie, also known as Mia Ventura, has pleaded not guilty to charges stemming from allegations that she stole money and valuables from people she met through dating apps, including wealthy older men and younger women.
Prosecutors allege Lavie targeted victims in Westlake Village, West Hollywood, Los Angeles and Beverly Hills between 2023 and 2025, posing as a girlfriend or travel companion to gain access to their homes before stealing cash, jewelry and designer merchandise.
She is charged with two counts each of grand theft and unauthorized use of personal identifying information, along with one count each of first-degree residential burglary and first-degree residential burglary with a person present.
Lavie was ordered to stand trial following a preliminary hearing in March, but criminal proceedings were suspended in August after her attorney raised concerns about her mental competency.
A judge had earlier denied a defense request for a mental health diversion program.
Lavie has remained in custody since July, when she was arrested while free on electronic monitoring. A judge subsequently denied bail.
She is also facing a separate criminal case in Riverside County involving allegations that she stole more than $11,000 worth of luxury items from an Airbnb rental during the 2025 Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival.
Lavie had been engaged to billionaire real estate investor and former gubernatorial candidate Stephen Cloobeck, who was arrested in May and charged with attempting to dissuade witnesses from testifying in the criminal case against her.
Cloobeck pleaded not guilty Aug. 7 to three felony counts involving alleged witness intimidation and a misdemeanor count of making annoying telephone calls.
The alleged victims named in the criminal complaint against Cloobeck are also alleged victims in Lavie’s case.
Lavie faces up to 11 years and eight months in state prison if convicted as charged in the Los Angeles County case, according to prosecutors.

The man made infamous as the "Tinder Swindler" wants to launch a dating app designed to keep users safe.
Simon Leviev, the name he goes by, became internationally notorious after a 2022 Netflix documentary detailed how women said they had been deceived and scammed through dating apps.
Now, according to 702/CapeTalk's Barbara Friedman, Leviev wants to launch his own dating app, called Safe Love.
And, unsurprisingly, the idea has caused quite a stir online.
Related articles:
‘You can’t make this up’
Friedman described the proposal as one of the more offbeat stories making the rounds, pointing out the apparent irony of Leviev wanting to create a dating app focused on safety.
"The man who allegedly scammed women out of millions of dollars on dating apps says he's reformed," she said.
Leviev reportedly says Safe Love will include several safety features, including ID checks, facial verification and an SOS feature intended to protect users from romance scammers and unsafe situations.
"He wants to launch a safe dating app," Friedman said. "And, of course, the internet is exploding over this."
She also said an organisation representing the online dating industry is calling for the proposed app to be stopped, with Apple and Google being urged to prevent it from appearing in their app stores.
‘Who better to educate women from getting scammed?’
The proposal prompted plenty of scepticism from the presenters.
"You can't make this up," Friedman said.
CapeTalk’s Clarence Ford joked: "Who are the best cybersecurity experts? Hackers."
"Well, there you go. Maybe he's on to something," came the response.
"He knows the tricks of the trade," added Ford.
Friedman said the reaction online had included comments such as "are we being punked?", while others questioned whether the app should be supported at all.
"That’s a no from me," she said.
She also pointed to Leviev's history with the law, saying he had been sentenced to several years in prison in three different countries.
Dating apps are now part of everyday life
The conversation also turned to how dramatically dating has changed since the emergence of dating apps.
One presenter said he had never used a dating app, while Friedman recalled using one in the late 2000s.
She said dating apps had become part of everyday life for younger people.
"It’s a way to meet people that you would never meet," she said.
But when it comes to a dating app launched by the man known as the Tinder Swindler, the presenters appeared considerably less enthusiastic.
As one of them put it, the question of whether to download it was unequivocal:
"She will absolutely unequivocally not download the app."

As a single woman, Kristina DeMichele, then 31, was thrilled to be able to buy her own house in Massachusetts — in the sought-after suburb of Melrose, no less. She purchased the two-bedroom, one-bath bungalow in 2021, and launched straight into making it hers — working with a designer to select furniture and arrange her art just so. Now that she had a yard, she toyed with the idea of getting a golden retriever.
All the while, she dreamed of moving out.
“I thought to myself, If my life goes the way I want it to, I will probably be selling this some time within five years,” she says.
Kristina wanted to get married, and her new space wouldn’t do for a family. She spent years on dating apps, looking for someone “warm, friendly, who would be a good listener.”
But the process was exhausting. “It was a lot of dates,” she says, which ultimately went nowhere.
Meanwhile, in Woburn, Andy Donato was feeling the same way. As 2022 wound down, Andy, then 36, decided to take a break from the apps. But he had one last date lined up, with a woman he’d connected with on Bumble: Kristina DeMichele. On the Sunday after Thanksgiving, they met for coffee at Cibo Cafe in Wakefield.
“We chatted for hours,” says Kristina, who had moved to Boston from Dublin, Ohio, in 2013 for a graduate program at Emerson College.
Both she and Andy were struck by how different the other had seemed from the other matches they’d met. “He had this sunshine yellow energy about him,” says Kristina. Their connection “was just so apparent from the beginning.”
Andy, also looking for a serious relationship, appreciated that Kristina was clear about what she wanted. “There was no leaving me guessing,” he says.
As the date was ending, he worried there might be a deal breaker: He had plans to adopt a puppy — a golden retriever — the next day. Did she like dogs? Kristina, of course, couldn’t wait to meet 4-month-old Minfilia, whom Andy had named after a character in Final Fantasy XIV — and to see Minnie’s owner again.
Two days later, Kristina brought pizza, and Andy introduced her to Minnie, their “dog-ter,” as they call her now. They shared their first kiss that night — “She was the one to make the first move,” he says. “I was like, Well, this is a communication style I could respect.”
Soon after, Andy brought Minnie to Kristina’s house, and helped put up her Christmas tree. The visit left an impression: “Seeing him as a dog dad and the way he was with her . . . when at this point too I’m thinking, I want a good father for my future child.”
The couple started seeing each other more often, cooking dinners after work — she was a digital content strategist for Harvard Magazine, while Andy was operations manager for his family’s Watertown-based heating and air conditioning supply business — at Kristina’s house. They’d experiment with Blue Apron recipes, then watch a science fiction film or a TV show — Game Changer is a favorite. Andy introduced Kristina to Star Wars, and video games. He gave her a Nintendo Switch, and they played Stardew Valley together.
By January, they were officially boyfriend and girlfriend. The relationship “just grew naturally,” Kristina says.
“I was optimistic, very hopefully optimistic,” says Andy.
They took turns making the 20-minute drive between Kristina’s in Melrose, and Andy’s condo in Woburn. Andy — “my ideas man,” as she calls him — began to offer Kristina advice on Kristini’s Teas, her herbal tea business that grew out of the pandemic, when she would research herbs that helped the immune system, and make custom blends for friends. The business “was born out of me discovering who I wanted to be as a person,” she says.
The couple attended weekend farmers markers, selling her product; in summer, she frequented farms to harvest locally grown herbs, and spent free time taking courses, attending seminars, and pouring through books to educate herself on medicinal properties. “It really brings me joy,” she says.
A year into dating, in November 2023, Andy moved in with Kristina. The next summer, he began working with a jeweler on a custom engagement ring. He hid the ring away until November, when they went to dinner at Mooo. . . . Beacon Hill for their second anniversary. Afterward, Andy suggested a walk through Boston Common, toward the Public Garden. “When I was going to grad school, I lived in Back Bay for six years, so this area is very special to me,” she says. They got to the lagoon footbridge, and Andy dropped to one knee, asking, “Are you ready to take your next walk with me?”
After getting engaged, the couple bought a single-family home in Woburn, where Andy has lived all of his life, moving two houses down from his parents. Kristini’s Teas, which is now sold in about 10 stores, was featured on Chronicle in March. “It utterly changed everything for the business. It’s been wonderful,” says Kristina, who is now assistant director of digital marketing at MIT Sloan.
And the celebrations continued, as the couple planned “a big Italian-Irish family bonanza,” inviting 220 people to the Beauport Hotel Gloucester for their May 24, 2026, wedding. Minnie served as the “ring bearer doggy,” and Andy’s cousin officiated.
The couple penned their own vows: Kristina promised to be Andy’s “witchy warrior woman,” and “to make space for his lightness” when life feels heavy. Andy vowed to keep her from working too hard, and to always be a good listener.
Growing up in Ohio, Kristina took saxophone lessons for 10 years, starting at age 9, and was later part of her college band at the University of Dayton in Ohio. Her childhood saxophone teacher flew in to provide the ceremony music, playing jazz classics and “The Very Thought of You,” one of her grandmother’s favorites, as Kristina walked down the aisle.
Later, the bride surprised her groom by playing a duet of “Blue Skies” with her former teacher to open the dance floor — one of her most cherished moments of the night.
A DJ provided reception music. The couple chose “Yellow” by Coldplay, a nod to her first impressions of Andy, for their first dance.
They decided on a three-week honeymoon in Italy — “We’re both history nerds,” Kristina says — with a special connection. “We took a trip to my Nonno’s village,” Kristina says, referring to her grandfather who died in 2025, “in the mountains of Puglia, with 600 people. . . . My grandfather’s brother was the parish priest for 30 years. Seven generations of my family are from this village.” He had given the couple a map, and “highlighted everywhere he ever lived or loved to go” — and Andy and Kristina followed.
Back in Woburn, they are settling into married life. Kristina looks forward to having a garden, so she can harvest her own herbs. And, as she had hoped back in 2021, her Melrose bungalow is on the market.

item.content:encoded:
Six years after launching Christian dating app Upward, the conglomerate Match Group is relaunching it as a marriage-focused app for young singles. Upward is now centered around "modern courtship."
"For a generation told to keep things casual and see where they go, saying you want marriage can almost feel countercultural," said Lauren DeFord, director of brand marketing at Match Group, in a press release shared with Mashable. "Built for people dating with marriage in mind, Upward is a home for singles who know what they want, hold strong standards and believe dating should lead somewhere."
The shift comes amid a deluge of "tradwife" content on social media, of young women rejecting (or claiming to reject) modern attitudes for more traditional gender roles in their relationships. The trend has reached a new peak in 2026 with Yesteryear, a novel about a tradwife influencer who wakes up in 1855, which has been on the New York Times bestsellers list for 23 weeks.
You May Also Like
AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections
Tinder — top pick for finding hookups
Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups
For several years, young adults have also been decrying hookup culture and casual sex, while also reportedly having less sex than in generations past.
Politics also reflects this cultural moment: The Trump administration is encouraging women to have more children while restricting reproductive rights.
And, according to data, young adults want to tie the knot. Match's recent Singles in America survey found that 72 percent of Gen Z want to get married. Match Group research also found that around one in four U.S. singles between 18 and 34 strongly identify with traditional values around family, faith, and community.
"Many countries in the world have matrimony apps, and for whatever reason, the U.S. has never really had one," Match Group's global chief marketing officer, Stephanie Danzi, told Mashable in a Zoom interview. "Upward was almost naturally emerging as a bit of a matrimonial app by the way that people were using it."
Danzi works specifically with the Everyone Everywhere portfolio, which includes affinity dating apps like Upward, Salams (for Muslim users), and HER (for Sapphic users).
At a time when Gen Z is frustrated by the dating scene — particularly dating apps — Match is betting on Upward to fill a gap.
Hinge vs. Upward
Hinge, another app in Match Group's portfolio, is "designed to be deleted." Both apps are relationship-focused, Danzi said, but what makes Upward different is its focus on marriage specifically and the timeline for marriage users are looking for.
"Whereas people on Hinge are there with certainly high intent and positive intent, on Upward, it's nearly...99 percent of people want kids," she said. "Essentially, all people are looking for marriage specifically, and for them, marriage is not an if, it's a when."
The average time from match to marriage for an anecdotal sample of couples who met on Upward (and wrote to Match about their relationship) was under one year.
"We hear from our users that they actually feel like they're coming on too strong on an app like Hinge because they are so marriage and kid-oriented," she said. But on Upward, it's the price of entry.
New features for the dating app 'with marriage in mind'
While Upward's users are predominantly Christian (given that it was a Christian dating app), Match found that the defining factor was less about religiosity and more about what family looks like and being goal-oriented towards marriage and family.
"On Upward, what we saw is that actually a lot of our prompts that were around, for example, 'what's your favorite Bible verse,' were actually not that popular, and people were spending a lot more time talking about what they wanted out of a family and out of the future," Danzi explained. People of all faiths are welcome on the app, and it's a young crowd: Match told Mashable that the majority of users are under 35.
In addition to refocusing Upward towards marriage, Match has also refreshed the app experience. It now includes "Chivalry Mode," an opt-in experience for users who prefer a more "traditional" first-move dynamic.
When both users in a match opt-in, the man is encouraged to send the first message (and a "high-quality" one, not just "Hey, what's up?"), and his match chooses whether to respond or unmatch. (Gay users are also welcome on Upward, and there are gay users on the app, Danzi said.) The second user then has 72 hours to respond.
As Danzi told Mashable, a man sending the first message isn't compulsory in Chivalry Mode, but the team has seen that the opt-in feature leads to more conversations.
Recently, the dating app Bumble changed its rules so that male users can message female ones first, after launching in 2014 as a "feminist" dating app where "women make the first move."
Also new is the Marriage Timeline feature, which lets users share when they hope to get married — and they can see other users' timelines, as well.
Users can also pick their "Core Values" on the app so potential matches can see their priorities, such as honor, wisdom, integrity, hard work, community, and friendship. According to Match, nearly every Upward member between 18 and 30 surveyed said they want a family, and "family" is the most-selected Core Value on the app. (On other Match Group apps, like Tinder and Hinge, you can signal lifestyle traits and what you're looking for.)
"The old checklist was height and income," Danzi said. "And the new checklist is about values."
Anna Iovine is the associate editor of features at Mashable. Previously, as the sex and relationships reporter, she covered topics ranging from dating apps to pelvic pain. Before Mashable, Anna was a social editor at VICE and freelanced for publications such as Slate and the Columbia Journalism Review. Follow her on Instagram.

item.content:encoded:
Love is in the air, and Big Love Tech—yes, really—is betting on “traditional values” to bring people back to dating apps.
Match Group, the tech behemoth behind Hinge, Tinder, and other abysmal programs to supposedly find love, is expanding its Christian-based app Upward to cater to people who fall into the trad-wife, or trad-husband, culture.
According to a press release by Upward, 72% of Gen Zers want to get married, an increase from previous generations.
“For a generation told to keep things casual and see where they go, saying you want marriage can almost feel countercultural,” Lauren DeFord, director of brand marketing at Match Group, said in the release. “Built for people dating with marriage in mind, Upward is a home for singles who know what they want, hold strong standards and believe dating should lead somewhere.”
The app also features a “chivalry mode,” where men are encouraged to make the first move.
Now, everyone has heard someone complaining about the difficulties of dating today or sharing how they’ve ditched the dating apps once and for all … only to return months later. But this shift from the tech Cupid overlords speaks to a larger movement being promoted within the political right: so-called traditional family structures and the elusive stay-at-home “tradwife.”
Looking toward an idyllic past in which a single income supplied family vacations and a backyard for three bouncing, healthy children, MAGA personalities like Vice President JD Vance and Katie Miller, the podcasting wife of White House aide Stephen Miller, have pushed this lifestyle as a necessity.
“I want more babies in the United States of America,” Vance said in his first address as vice president.
Then again, with the price of a pound of lean ground beef higher than the federal minimum wage, the vision of a white picket fence and an apple pie on the window sill is more likely to be AI-generated slop than a living reality for many Americans.
Related | Who’s questioning women’s right to vote?
And all this exhaustion from the nation’s affordability dumpster-fire has resulted in exactly what MAGA personalities have hoped for: women’s retreat from the workforce in hopes of having a less chaotic life. More than 455,000 women left the workforce between January and August 2025, according to data from the nonprofit Catalyst.
We can see this push for women to retreat into the throes of submissive wifehood within the Trump administration. Second lady Usha Vance, a once-successful lawyer, stepped down from her role, and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was pushing for wives to give up their right to vote. And conservative commentators began preaching about the dangers of femininity in the workplace.
Worse, this push has come amid the Trump administration’s refusal to support families with meaningful legislation, like an increased child tax credit or universal paid family leave.
Now Match Group is seeking to cash in on the hopes that people want a clear timeline to marriage and a traditional partner with traditional values. But while the desire for a more “traditional” love may be in the air, that doesn’t mean that the government around them caters to that life, either.

item.content:encoded:
They grew up swiping, but Manchester’s twentysomethings are ghosting dating apps in favour of an old-school solution making a comeback across the city: speed dating.
Mid20s, founded by Jonah Gray and Evie Carricker, has sold out all 41 of its speed dating events for 23 to 27-year-olds since launching in the city last summer.
Their events have attracted more than 1,000 Mancunian singles, who have collectively been on over 5,000 dates, resulting in more than 400 romantic matches.
Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter
The idea came after Jonah and Evie, who met by chance on a coach from Bristol to Manchester, bonded over their frustrations with modern dating culture and the lack of opportunities for young people to meet in person.
Jonah, who previously organised music events and raves, said the pair shared a disdain for dating apps that led them to create an alternative to digital dating for young people.
“What was at first maybe a nice idea, and maybe seemed like something that could help connect people, has now made people even further apart,” he said.
“There’s an abundance of choice, and I think it creates this real expendable viewpoint of a person.”
He said in-person speed dating solved that problem.
“Within five minutes, you’ve met someone, had a chat. On paper, you’re dating 12 people for the price of one.
“You’re being precious with your time and energy whilst meeting loads of people.”
Demand for the events has grown quickly. What began as a single Manchester night now runs close to fortnightly in the city and has expanded to Sheffield and Leeds, with tickets regularly selling out within minutes of release.
Each event typically hosts around 30 people, who take part in five-minute dates with other attendees. At the end of the night, guests submit the names of up to three people they would like to see again romantically.
But the founders said the friendships formed at the events had become just as significant as the romantic matches.
“I think we underestimated how much of it that would be,” Evie said.
“We’ve got huge groups of people who’ve all met through our events.”
They said feedback had been overwhelmingly positive, with 91 per cent of attendees rating their experience five stars and groups often continuing to socialise well beyond the scheduled dating slots.
The pair also vet every attendee before issuing tickets in a bid to create a safe and welcoming environment. “It’s amazing how consistently lovely the people we attract are,” Jonah said.
The founders said they hoped more people who were hesitant about attending would give the events a try.
“I just wish people who were on the fence would just do it,” Jonah said. “We get so many people who say they were so nervous, they almost dropped out, and then they had a brilliant time. The worst thing that’ll happen is you end up with a funny story for the group chat,” Evie added.
The next Mid20s Manchester event, for lesbian, bisexual and queer women, will take place on Tuesday, September 22 at To Be Frank. A further event for men and women is planned for October 14 at Side Street.
Events are ticketed, with details available by messaging @mid__twenties on Instagram.

item.content:encoded:
The trouble with dating apps is that the carousel never stops. How can anyone make a considered decision about Daisy from Putney when Julia from Richmond is a thumb-twitch away? And somewhere behind Julia, surely, is someone even better. After years of swiping, the patient zero of our interminable romantic misery, the apps, are finally in their death rattle. If they achieved one thing, it’s uniting the world against them.
With the apps came dating insanity. I’ve had my fair share. One match popped up with a gallery of elegant, charismatic photos and a profile Jane Austen could have written. She turned out not to be in her late thirties, as the beautiful prose suggested, but in her mid to late seventies. How did she get away with it? Simple. She’d used her daughter’s photos because, in her words: “I get more matches that way.”
Can’t argue with that. Over the froth of my seemingly never-ending cappuccino, I asked: “But… does it work?” “Oh yes,” she said. “I’ve had loads of fun with younger men.” To be fair to her, the sex was fantastic (kidding). And she wasn’t even the strangest. There was the beautiful woman who took me back to her Surrey mansion, where her husband was waiting in the hallway, in a leather armchair, naked from the waist down.
Apps are a dopamine drip that never runs dry but they don’t actually work because romance was never going to be found by searching. It grows out of attraction and chemistry, one of the few parts of being human that still feels like magic.
I’m not alone in retiring my exhausted digits. In a single year, Tinder, Hinge and Bumble lost more than a million UK users between them. And the people my age who hang on are the most devoted of all. 55- to 64-year-olds on dating apps spend nearly six hours on them in a month, longer than any other age group. That’s a lot of evenings scrolling past partners in crime.
And it’s mostly men doing the swiping: more than six in 10 people using dating services in the UK are male, which will surprise no woman with thumbs. What men get wrong is written all over their profiles. In my work helping people in acute emotional pain, break-up and divorce, I hear from women who are on the apps even in their heartbreak. The relentless draw of the next swipe keeps them chasing the dating app dragon, and they end up drowning in a sea of clichés. If men say they want “no drama, no time-wasters”, they are talking about their last relationship, not hopes for the next one.
Apps are having to adapt too. Tinder has introduced an “events” tab where users can choose to go on real-life dates, from trivia nights to ceramics classes. So, the company that invented “the swipe”, now wants you in a room with other people, making a wonky mug.
These days I give relationship advice to more than 400,000 women on social media. I’ve heard it all: the ghosting, the man who messaged for three weeks and never once suggested a coffee, the profile photos with the ex badly cropped out. I’ve built a whole part of my business offering advice on meeting people in real life.
So, if you’re ready to put the phone down, here’s where I’d start.
Go somewhere more than once. A weekly class, a choir, a walking group, a volunteering shift. The first week you’re a stranger. By the fourth, you’re a familiar face. Attraction often grows out of simply seeing someone regularly.
Choose things you would enjoy even if you met nobody. If the only point of the evening is finding someone, every evening without them is a failure. If you’d happily go anyway, you’re relaxed and better company. Nobody has ever been charmed by someone gritting their teeth through salsa.
Take a friend, then talk to other people. Arriving with someone makes walking through the door easier. Just make a rule before you go in, so you don’t spend the whole evening talking only to each other.
Say yes to the invitations you’d normally dodge. The 50th birthday, the leaving drinks, the barbecue at the house of a friend of a friend. An awful lot of good relationships still start with someone saying: “You must meet my friend.”
If you do stay on the apps, put them in their place. Set a time limit, check them at set times rather than all evening and move to meeting in person quickly. A week of messaging tells you far less than 20 minutes over a coffee.
The swipe had a good run. But it made us fussy, and a little greedy, always sure someone better was one flick away. My seventysomething coffee date understood the game better than any of us: the apps reward the picture, and she’d simply borrowed a better one. The rest of us might do better turning up, again and again, until someone notices.

item.content:encoded:
It’s no secret that everyone is a little tired of dating apps. In 2024, research showed that consistent users of these apps were experiencing burnout symptoms. If you’ve ever spent 30 minutes swiping left on a sea of cringe prompt responses and pictures of men holding fish, you’re not surprised at this. Conversations seem to go nowhere, people feel very brave saying unhinged things to each other through a screen, and everyone is lying about their height.
Throwing in a subscription fee on top of that? No.
We get it: Businesses need to make money. But when a dating app hides its best features—you know, the ones that actually help you get a date—behind a paywall, it makes a user a lot less likely to want to keep swiping.
And while plenty of apps have jumped on this capitalistic train of “selling” love, not all of them have left their users with the scraps of the apps.
There are still some dating apps that are letting users look for love without having to plug in their credit card information. So you’re free (literally) to focus on what’s important: finding someone you think you could tolerate enough to go on a date with IRL.
Facebook Dating
Okay, the idea of still being on Facebook is daunting enough, so I understand the hesitation of dating on it. But as someone who has tried Facebook Dating in the past, I have to say it’s actually a pretty good dating platform. And if you’re worried that it’s just a means of dating people you “friended” in high school, it’s not.
It has a free matching and messaging experience, and if you already have Facebook downloaded you don’t have to worry about adding another app to your phone.
Feeld
If you’re looking for a dating experience outside of the norms of modern-day courting, Feeld is a great (and free) option. It’s for people looking to explore everything from nonmonogamy to casual hookups and other relationship styles. You can create a profile, connect with mutual likes, and chat—all without paying. While there are tiers that require a subscription, those just come with unlimited likes and the option to see who liked you.
Hinge
Okay, Hinge is definitely an app that has some features locked behind a payment but the app still offers a lot of great options for people who don’t want to whip out their credit card. The free version of the app gives you all of the essentials: browsing profiles, sending likes, matching, and chatting with matches. Just keep in mind that there’s a daily like limit (but I’ve never reached it, so you’ll be fine).
Tinder
Tinder is probably going to give you the biggest possible dating pool—and a lot of that access is for free. You can create a profile, like people, match, and message for free. The only thing to note is that using the paid option will give you access to premium prompts and the ability to set certain preferences.
Bumble
All of Bumble’s basic features (including its safety verification ones) are totally free when you download the app. This means you can find matches and—if you identify as a woman—message first all for free. The app lets you have safe, meaningful interactions without having to pay a dime.
OkCupid
If you want more than three photos and some prompts to base your swipe on, OkCupid is a great option. It’s free tier includes compatibility-focused profiles and extensive questions so you’re really getting a good idea of who someone is before you match with them.

Senate clears Blackburn-backed bill requiring dating app fraud alerts
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WZTV) — The U.S. Senate has passed a bipartisan bill backed by Tennessee Sen. Marsha Blackburn that would require dating apps to alert some users when an account that messaged them is banned for suspected financial fraud.
The Senate passed H.R. 2481, known as the Romance Scam Prevention Act, without amendment by unanimous consent on Sept. 23. The House passed the measure in June 2025, meaning the bill now heads to President Donald Trump.
Blackburn, a Republican, introduced Senate companion legislation with Democratic Sen. John Hickenlooper of Colorado. The measure that cleared Congress was introduced in the House by Republican Rep. David Valadao of California.
If signed, the law would take effect one year after enactment.
Under the bill, an online dating service would have to send a fraud-ban notification to a user who received a message from an account that was later banned because the service determined there was a significant risk the account holder would try to fraudulently obtain money.
MORE NEWS | New Tennessee poll shows Blackburn with big lead, Trump's approval underwater
The requirement would not apply to every person who may have interacted with the account. The bill specifically refers to users who received a message from the banned account through the dating service.
The notice would need to identify the banned account and tell the recipient when they most recently sent or received a message with that user. It also would need to warn that the person may have used a false identity or attempted to defraud users, advise people not to send cash or financial information and provide fraud-prevention resources and customer-service contact information.
Dating apps generally would have 24 hours after issuing a fraud ban to send the notice. The bill allows an app to take up to three days in some circumstances and permits longer delays if requested by law enforcement during an active investigation.
RELATED COVERAGE | Man accused of posing as 49ers player in $1.3M romance scam seen in video
The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the law, while state attorneys general and other authorized state consumer-protection officials could bring civil actions.
The legislation focuses on a common way romance scammers try to build trust before seeking money. The FTC reported that nearly 70,000 people reported romance scams in 2022, with reported losses reaching $1.3 billion.
But dating apps are only one route scammers use. Among 2022 romance-scam loss reports that identified a contact method, the FTC said 40% began on social media and 19% began on a website or app.
In Tennessee, the FBI reported that people 60 and older filed 1,577 fraud complaints in 2023 and reported losing about $43.75 million. That was up from about $36.57 million in reported losses in 2022 — an increase of roughly 19.6%.
Those Tennessee figures include all reported fraud types involving people 60 and older, not romance scams alone.
The FTC advises people not to send cash, gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency to someone they know only online. Suspicious profiles or messages can be reported to the dating app and to ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

item.content:encoded:
Matchmaking is having a moment, whether it's an AI matchmaker for college students or human matchmakers with decades of experience. And while singles are increasingly vexed by dating apps, the platforms are trying to pull in loved ones to help them date, too — like with Hinge's recent feature Friend's Take.
Amid these trends, a new app for both singles and wannabe matchmakers launches today: Rivet. Founded by former Tinder and Match Group executive Taru Kapoor, Rivet is a "social matching" app that will attempt to replace algorithms with the wisdom of crowds. Users sign up as Daters or Matchers, and all are encouraged to pair up others.
"Dating has always been social," said Kapoor in a press release shared with Mashable. She spent years thinking that dating apps were removing friction from meeting each other, but instead, "we removed the people."
You May Also Like
AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections
Tinder — top pick for finding hookups
Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups
Dating apps created matches by connecting people who wouldn't have met otherwise, Kapoor continued, but a side effect was that they turned something fundamentally social and human — dating — into a transactional, isolated activity.
"I built Rivet to change that," she said. "Rivet is built on a simple truth: humans understand chemistry and compatibility in a way that no algorithm can. You don't have to find your person entirely on your own, let people help you find your person."
How does Rivet work?
On Rivet, all Daters are also Matchers, but not all Matchers are Daters, Kapoor told Mashable. "Even if you're married, in a relationship or simply not currently looking to date, you can still join Rivet to be a Matcher and help people find meaningful connections," she said over email. You can make a Dater profile later if you'd like, but you're never required to.
Matchers provide their opinions on potential pairs and recommend introductions for users they believe would be a good couple. Pairs who receive high "Social Matching scores" are then introduced to each other on the app, and each person decides whether to match and start a conversation.
You can be on Rivet solely as a Dater, Kapoor continued, though the app encourages Daters to participate in matching others.
More than two-thirds (68 percent) of Gen Z and millennials said they'd be interested in helping someone they don't personally know find a potential romantic match (if they can do so anonymously, and the pair themselves made the final decision), according to a national survey of over 2,000 U.S. adults commissioned by Rivet.
And some prizes can sweeten the deal, too. Matchers can receive rewards for helping people find love, according to Rivet's website. "Match a pair that you think will click or call a mismatch, and you earn Karma. Karma gets you bragging rights and can be redeemed for rewards," it states.
Currently, reaching 15,000 Karma with a strong MQ (Matcher Quotient, the app's way of displaying a Matcher's thoughtfulness and accuracy) can be redeemed for $30 equivalent in cash or gift cards, Kapoor said. The team is working on making more reward and redemption options available soon.
Those with high MQ might also be bestowed as Elite Matchers.
In addition to the app, Rivet also hosts live events, such as a dating show in New York City in early Oct.
More dating apps are adding AI — meaning, more algorithms — and Rivet is bucking the trend. It's now available for free on iOS and Android.
Anna Iovine is the associate editor of features at Mashable. Previously, as the sex and relationships reporter, she covered topics ranging from dating apps to pelvic pain. Before Mashable, Anna was a social editor at VICE and freelanced for publications such as Slate and the Columbia Journalism Review. Follow her on Instagram.

item.content:encoded:
One of the worst sentences a girl’s friend group can hear is, “I downloaded Hinge again.” Generally, this can be excused following a breakup, but at its worst, it’s a woman defying her own logic and reasoning while crafting excuses for her horrible situationship “Because obviously, he’s super busy and nobody else understands.”
Despite arguments that having a boyfriend is currently a social faux pas, people still seek connection. Additionally, straight women’s dating frustrations have generated numerous pop albums, and even their own term, heterofatalism. Heterofatalism, coined by Asa Seresin, a sexuality scholar, describes the phenomenon of straight women feeling embarrassed about their attraction toward men and desire to detach themselves from the world of dating and subsequent disappointment.
I don’t think the issue here is that men simply suck. Nor do I think the death of chivalry is entirely to blame. Dating apps may be part of the problem. With a large selection of profiles, dating app users are more likely to reject the profiles accessible to them. Women experiencing this rejection mindset are less likely to obtain matches. Despite access to more potential partners on dating apps, the act of choosing the right partner isn’t as clear.
Sam Kizer, assistant professor of instruction in sociology at Ohio University, recognizes the influence of assistive technology in modern dating. He discussed the various dating resources marketed towards single people, including cards to bring to a date encouraging face-to-face conversations, dating apps and generative artificial intelligence.
“The algorithm, the tech, the dating, the cards, the apps, the cards, whatever, they might be able to assist in finding people to evaluate,” Kizer said. “They themselves cannot be the evaluator.”
Although dating apps create an opportunity to meet new people and potentially introduce users to new labels or types of relationships, the mere act of creating a profile requires the user to exclude potential matches to some degree. On Hinge, if you say you’re looking for a long-term relationship, the algorithm within the app is already curating who is and isn’t available for you as a potential match.
Alongside dating app usage, increased AI use in daily life, from email writing to LinkedIn job searches, hinders their ability to make independent critical decisions. Effective communication skills are vital to healthy relationships; this becomes an issue with a growing number of people using generative AI chatbots to analyze and support their relationship decisions.
Generation Z has faced numerous barriers to healthy social development, leading to an increase in social anxiety and loneliness. Utilizing online spaces to meet people can mitigate potential fear of rejection, but these online connections are not likely to help people feel less lonely.
Dating is meant to feel good, and it’s not surprising even pop music artists are calling out when it doesn't. Human connection is messy, vulnerable and cannot be calculated by an app or algorithm. Even if you or your best friend resorts to redownloading dating apps once again, try to remember taking a risk against your typical standards or expectations might not be so risky.
Alexa Sanders is a senior studying psychology at Ohio University. Please note the opinions expressed in this column do not represent those of The Post. Want to talk to Alexa about her column? Email her at al683822@ohio.edu.

The rising cost of living has impacted singles for years now, and a new report from payment service Zelle shares new insights on just how much their bank accounts influence how (and if) they find love.
Zelle's Economics of Dating Report found that the vast majority (84 percent) of Gen Z and millennial daters say rising cost has affected their dating lives (according to an Aug. 2026 national survey of 1,800 Gen Z and millennial adults who've dated within the past year).
Around a third (32 percent) said they're going on fewer dates, and one in 10 (11 percent) have stopped dating because they can't afford it.
You May Also Like
AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections
Tinder — top pick for finding hookups
Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups
As Mashable reported this year, socioeconomic factors can definitely hinder dating. Not only can some young people not afford dates, but more are living at home and can't buy a home. This can then delay when people get married and have children.
But for those young adults still in the dating pool, Zelle's report found that some respondents are choosing less expensive activities (40 percent), preferring more frequent economical dates to occasional expensive ones (38 percent), and suggesting free activities (37 percent).
And in this economy, being seen as frugal is a good thing. Thirty-eight percent said they judged someone positively for planning an affordable, thoughtful date — more than the 23 percent who said the same for someone who put together an extravagant, high-end one.
Other financial green flags include being thoughtful with money (56 percent), being honest and transparent about money (54 percent), planning a thoughtful, budget-friendly date (52 percent), and paying without making the situation awkward (52 percent).
On the flipside, there are some red flags when it comes to money and dating, such as making someone uncomfortable about what they can afford, expecting the other person to pay for everything, complaining about every price, and talking too much about income — all of which 47 percent of participants said gave them the ick. Around the same amount, 46 percent, also flagged making a big deal about paying.
Money anxiety abounds these days, including when trying to find a partner. Among women respondents, being rejected and spending too much ranked equally as sources of dating anxiety (37 percent). Other sources of anxiety are spending too much on a date (34 percent of participants said this), making sure a date fits within their budget (29 percent), discussing finances (28 percent), and asking who pays (25 percent).
Twenty-six percent said they won't bring up payment with their date at all.
This all seems like glum news, but at least 89 percent of daters are still putting themselves out there. There are dating apps you can use for free and low-cost outings, too, like a walk in the park. Otherwise, some singles might find themselves turning to AI for a cheaper date.

item.content:encoded:
Dating apps don’t exactly have the best rep right now. Apps have seen a drop in users and just this month TIME declared that they are dead.
Everyone has their own guess as to why swiping feels slightly cringe: People want to make in-person connections, they think everyone on the apps is ugly, and, importantly users—mostly women—just don’t feel safe.
While I am a dating app retiree, I still vividly remember the amount of unhinged and frankly, frightening messages I received from men while on the apps. I know girlfriends who have been catfished, threatened, and even borderline stalked by men they swiped right on (and even ones they didn’t).
The people behind the apps are aware of the safety concerns and some (not all) have taken real steps to make sure their users feel as comfortable as possible—because trying to find love online is already difficult enough without having to worry about some creep using AI photos to trick you into meeting up.
So if you’re looking to swipe without worrying about your safety, here are some of the safest dating apps out there. Unfortunately, you’re on your own when it comes to what your matches look like.
Bumble
Despite the fact that I would never message a man first, Bumble is really steps ahead of a lot of other dating apps. They have one of the most extensive set of user-facing safety tools out there: photo verification, optional ID verification, and in-app voice and video calls. It also has the Share Date feature, which lets you share the details of an upcoming date with a trusted friend or family member. Plus, it blurs out potentially explicit photos, allows you to block, report, and unmatch someone, and even has a Deception Detector for users that are flagged as potential fake or scam accounts. It really gives you a lot of ways to vet someone before ever handing over your number.
Tinder
Tinder’s reputation has come a long way. What used to be known as “the hookup app” is now a pretty decent place to get to know someone—all while staying safe.
The app requires a Face Check, photo verification, Share My Date (similar to Bumble), and of course the ability to block and report someone. What really makes it a great option is the fact that users are prompted with “Are You Sure?” and “Does This Bother You?” message interventions to prompt people to think before they send something inappropriate, as well as the chance to report if something crosses the line.
Hinge
Hinge has become a lot more aggressive lately when it comes to authenticating its users. Its Face Check includes a video selfie and liveness check, which is then compared to profile photos. This can help detect duplicate or scam accounts.
Hinge’s Help Center also includes a variety of articles on “Safe Dating,” including pieces on consent, boundaries, and how to protect yourself from scammers.
Coffee Meets Bagel
Coffee Meet Bagel has always been known as a dating app for people who are really intentional about dating. And now, it has a bunch of safety features to make that more possible. The app has a live selfie verification—which has been completed by 70 percent of its users.
Match
Match focuses on moderation and user safety. Like some of the other apps on this list, it offers blocking, human moderation, anti-harassment measures, and privacy controls that lets users set who can contact them and what info goes on their profile. The app also gives users the chance to flag specifically for fake profiles, requests for money, and other violations.
