item.content:encoded:
A recent study suggests that a woman’s level of religious belief influences how she evaluates potential partners on swipe-based dating apps like Tinder. When navigating these platforms, women often face a trade-off between evaluating a potential partner’s genetic fitness and their willingness to invest in a relationship. The findings indicate that more religious women show a broader initial receptivity to men’s profiles, while overall, women tend to prefer softer facial features but surprisingly favor exaggerated, unverifiable profile biographies. The research was published in Psychology & Sexuality.
Swipe-based dating applications require users to make split-second decisions about potential partners based on a single photograph and a brief biography. These platforms compress mate selection into rapid, low-consequence choices, forcing users to rely heavily on highly visible cues. When evaluating a photograph, people often pick up on facial sexual dimorphism, which refers to how physically masculinized or feminized a face appears.
Earlier research discovered that women often prefer softer, feminized male faces over hyper-masculine ones. For instance, a 1998 study showed that women routinely find feminized male faces more attractive than strictly masculine alternatives. This preference exists partly because rugged features are linked to lower trustworthiness, with a 2012 study indicating that women view more masculine men as more likely to engage in unfaithful behavior.
Religious norms often emphasize long-term relational stability and sexual restraint. Supporting this, a study covered by PsyPost in 2017 indicated that higher religious commitment is associated with a greater preference for long-term mating strategies and fewer sexual partners. Because of this association, researchers expected that religious women might be more cautious when evaluating potential partners online.
The new study builds on this concept by examining how initial visual judgments interact with written profile details and a woman’s own religiosity on modern dating apps. The research was conducted by Katherine L. Sheetz, a Ph.D. candidate, and Lisa L. M. Welling, a professor of psychology, both at Oakland University.
“Online dating has changed the way people make initial judgments about potential partners, especially since the COVID-19 pandemic forced the majority of dating online,” Welling, who directs the Welling Research Lab, told PsyPost. “Swipe-based platforms reduce initial mate choice selections to very rapid decisions based on relatively limited visual and textual information, yet we know relatively little about how individual differences, such as religiosity, shape those early decisions.”
“With this study, we were particularly interested in religiosity because it is associated with sexual restraint, restricted sociosexuality (meaning lower openness to casual sex), and long-term relationship motivations on average,” Welling explained. “We therefore wanted to test whether more religious women would be more selective when evaluating potential male partners in an online context, particularly when profiles contained cues that could be relevant to apparent trustworthiness and relationship intentions.”
The study included 439 single cisgender women between the ages of 18 and 38 who were primarily attracted to men. The participants completed an online survey that began with questionnaires assessing their religious beliefs and their motivations for using dating applications. Afterward, they completed a simulated Tinder task where they viewed 20 distinct male dating profiles. Each profile featured a photograph of a smiling man and a short, 500-character biography.
The researchers manipulated the photographs using computer software so that the faces appeared either 50 percent more masculinized or 50 percent more feminized, while keeping skin tone and identity the same. The profile biographies were also written to be either trustworthy or untrustworthy.
Trustworthy biographies included verifiable, specific information regarding education or employment and avoided grand claims. Untrustworthy biographies featured exaggerated personal achievements and vague job descriptions, a tactic known as selective self-presentation. The participants had to either accept each profile, mimicking a right swipe, or reject the profile, mimicking a left swipe.
The researchers found that facial features strongly guided the women’s choices. Profiles featuring masculinized faces had approximately 56 percent lower odds of being accepted compared to profiles with feminized faces. However, the biographic text yielded unexpected results. Instead of favoring honest profiles, women showed a preference for the exaggerated text. Profiles with untrustworthy biographies had about 24 percent higher odds of acceptance compared to those with straightforward, trustworthy biographies.
“We were also surprised that profiles containing our ‘untrustworthy’ biographies were accepted more often than profiles containing the ‘trustworthy’ biographies,” Welling said. “The manipulation successfully changed perceptions of trustworthiness in the intended direction, so the finding suggests that participants may have been responding to other characteristics conveyed by those biographies, rather than simply preferring less trustworthy partners. We think it might have been something like perceived confidence in the untrustworthy bios because they tended to be more boastful.”
A woman’s level of religious belief also played a role in her swiping behavior, but not in the direction the researchers originally predicted. Higher religiosity predicted higher overall profile acceptance across the board. For each one-unit increase on the study’s seven-point religiosity scale, the odds of a profile being accepted increased by roughly 38 percent.
“The main takeaway is that religiosity was associated with greater initial receptivity to potential partners in our simulated online-dating task, rather than greater selectivity, which is the opposite of what we originally predicted,” Welling noted.
She cautioned that while the association was statistically reliable, it was not necessarily a massive shift in real-world behavior. “An odds ratio is not the same thing as saying that someone was 30% or 38% more likely to date someone,” Welling clarified. “The outcome in our study was simply whether a participant accepted a profile in a controlled, simulated swiping task. In other words, our findings suggest that religious women are more likely to be open to dating men with a greater range of characteristics, but not that they necessarily would accept more men after that initial swipe.”
In exploratory analyses, the researchers looked at why the women used dating apps in the first place. Women who used the apps with the goal of finding a relationship accepted fewer profiles overall, showing a 38 percent reduction in acceptance odds for each one-unit increase in relational motivation. Entertainment or exploratory motives for using the app had no statistical effect on acceptance rates.
The preference for exaggerated biographies is in tension with research covered by PsyPost in 2016, which found that dating profiles featuring heavy bragging reduced viewers’ intentions to contact the owner. This difference might be explained by how the new study was designed, as the simulated Tinder task measured immediate profile acceptance during rapid swiping rather than a deliberate intention to date the profile owner.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The simulated paradigm was not a fully interactive dating application, meaning real-world swiping behavior might differ. The acceptance of a profile in this specific task might reflect a general openness to new experiences or basic social interaction, rather than true romantic intent.
“The biggest caveat is that accepting a dating profile is not the same thing as choosing a partner, having sex with someone, entering a relationship, or taking a real-world interpersonal risk,” Welling emphasized. “Our measure captured an early-stage decision about whether a profile was sufficiently appealing to remain in consideration for potential further contact.”
She also warned against misinterpreting the biography finding as evidence that women prefer dishonest men. “Our biographies combined different aspects of self-presentation, including the extent to which information could theoretically be externally verified and the degree of selective self-presentation,” Welling explained. “Although they produced the intended differences in perceived trustworthiness, they may also have conveyed other characteristics, such as confidence… or like social status, that then influenced profile acceptance.”
The religiosity measure used in the study combined social elements, like attending religious services, with intrinsic elements, like personal beliefs. Social religiosity is often linked to higher interpersonal trust, which might explain the unexpectedly high acceptance rates among religious women. The study sample was also limited to young college-aged women in the United States, meaning the results might not automatically apply to other demographics.
Future research could use eye-tracking technology to see exactly which parts of a dating profile women pay the most attention to. Researchers might also separate different types of religious belief to better understand how they affect romantic risk-taking online. This would provide a better picture of how individuals navigate trust and uncertainty in the digital dating world.
“A major next step is to make the dating environment more realistic and to see how these findings translate into the in-person dating world,” Welling told PsyPost. “Our task captured the rapid decision-making aspect of swipe-based dating similar to dating apps like Tinder, but it was still a controlled simulation and results from face-to-face dating may differ.”
“I think the broader point is that online dating is an interesting setting for studying human decision-making because it makes the initial stages of mate evaluation unusually visible,” Welling concluded. “People are making rapid judgments from photographs, short biographies, and other limited cues, and those judgments reflect both characteristics of the profile and characteristics of the person doing the judging. Our findings suggest that we should be cautious about assuming that a characteristic associated with one aspect of mating psychology will necessarily predict behavior in another context.”
The study, “Holy swipes: the influence of religiosity on mate choice in online dating,” was authored by Katherine L. Sheetz and Lisa L. M. Welling.

My dating app experiences haven’t been great. There have been ghosters and time-wasters and people who seemed fun over text but couldn’t hold a conversation in person.
My friends, though, have had some real Hinge horror stories.
One went on a date with a guy who told her he was planning to write his PhD thesis on “the philosophy of woman” but somehow didn’t notice that he had been explaining it for 30 minutes without letting the woman across from him speak.
Another girl went on a date with someone who made her do their laundry, and pay for it. They claimed they had a new debit card that didn’t work and hadn’t been able to do their laundry for two weeks as a result.
And one friend experienced “Hinge-cest”, where she and all her friends had ended up dating the same men. There are “Hinge celebrities” who have gone on so many dates that their reputation precedes them.
Sounds like the ideal environment for meeting the love of your life, right?
Despite the technology’s poor reputation, it feels like everyone my age is on the apps. However, I only know a handful who have actually ended up in relationships with people they met online. Most, after weeks or months of scrolling, texting and going on dates, become frustrated and delete the app. And then, after failing to meet someone in real life, they re-download it.
So why are so many young people using dating apps if they don’t work? I believe it’s because my generation doesn’t know how to date in person.
Gen Z spent some of its formative dating and socialising years in lockdown, and we’ve grown up communicating over the internet. So it makes sense that this has had a lingering effect.
Dating apps seem to offer an easy way out. I do find it easier to speak to a new person online; shyness and awkwardness don’t come across over text. And perhaps most importantly, online rejection is far less humiliating.
But our dependence on dating apps might be making dating harder for us.
The idea that everyone is on Hinge has made making a move in person a completely foreign idea. Gen Z has lost the willingness to take a chance and just ask someone out, which dating has always relied on.
The gamification of dating makes us view it as a lazy activity – something we can do without leaving our bedrooms.
What’s worse is the horrible culture fostered by these apps. Ghosting people and talking to more than 10 people at once are considered normal. It’s no wonder users seem to forget they’re interacting with real humans. Similarly, your entire judgment of someone is based on a few photos.
None of this is conducive to genuine connection. It’s a tick-box model of dating, where you reject anyone who doesn’t fit your “ideal partner” criteria based on their photo and a few titbits of information. All this does is teach us to how to market ourselves to please other people and relentlessly judge others.
Dating in real life can be the opposite: you might end up with someone who doesn’t tick all the boxes you thought you wanted, but who ticks others that you didn’t realise you needed. The most important things, like real-life chemistry, communication style and personality, can’t be captured in a dating-app profile.
Although dating apps can have value for those who don’t have many opportunities to meet new people in real life, we need to break away from the mindset that they’re the only way to connect.
After the end of my last relationship, a friend told me to “keep going out, meeting new people, and something would happen eventually”. So, I made a conscious effort to say yes to every invitation that came my way – whether it was a spontaneous dinner, a side-quest that sends the night in a new direction, or a new book club. Even when I felt busy, or tired, or didn’t think I’d enjoy it.
And my life has become so much richer as a result. I’m meeting interesting people every day, going to places I haven’t been before, and trying out new things. Last week I spent an evening at a small art gallery in Brunswick, another at a themed house party, and a morning at a philosophy reading group. I’m much happier than I was when I was scrolling Hinge. And I know something will happen when it’s meant to.
I’m learning that dating in a meaningful way takes courage, patience and rejection – like it did for generations before mine. In any case, I think I’d still rather be rejected in real life than do an internet stranger’s washing on a first date.
Saria Ratnam is a University of Melbourne arts student.

item.content:encoded:
If you’re looking for a serious relationship, dating apps can start to feel like a particularly exhausting game of “What the hell are you actually looking for?” Sure, their profile says “long-term relationship,” but does that mean marriage? A committed partner? Someone to split a Costco membership with? Or someone who will text you “wyd” every Thursday night for the next six months?
The good news is that people absolutely do use dating apps to find real, long-term relationships. And while certain apps are designed to make finding a serious partner easier, there’s no single app that magically contains all the people ready to commit. “Any dating app or website can be good for long-term relationships if you are honest and intentional about what you want from the beginning,” says Rachel Needle, PsyD, a licensed psychologist and co-director of Modern Sex Therapy Institutes.
Still, choosing an app that attracts people looking for the same kind of relationship you are can save you a whole lot of time. Just as important is making your own intentions clear. Clinical sexologist Tatyannah King, MSW, recommends explicitly stating that you’re looking for something long-term in your profile, even if doing so means getting fewer matches. She also suggests including specific details that actually tell people something about your life and personality. Basically, you’re trying to find someone compatible, not collect every available human within a 15-mile radius.
Ready to get back out there? Below, we’re breaking down the best dating apps for serious relationships, who they’re best for, what they cost, and what you should know before downloading.
1. Bumble
Best For:
Women who want more control over how conversations start.
Why We Picked It:
“Bumble is an ideal app for people who are looking for long-term partnerships, especially for women who date men,” King says. “As someone who dates with intention and prefers long-term relationships over short flings, I’ve personally also found it helpful to pay for the premium version. I noticed that men who are paying for the premium version of Bumble’s dating app seem to be more intentional about dating.”
She also loves Bumble’s Opening Moves feature, which lets women set prompts that their matches can respond to, giving them another way to get a conversation going beyond sending the first message themselves. Matches expire if no one sends a message within 24 hours, which can help keep things moving instead of letting a promising match sit untouched for three weeks.
Who It’s For:
Bumble is open to daters of all genders and orientations. In heterosexual matches, women traditionally initiate the conversation, but Opening Moves gives them the option to set a prompt that a match can respond to instead. In same-gender and nonbinary connections, either person can start the conversation.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
Pros:
- Opening Moves gives women more flexibility over how conversations get started
- Snooze Mode lets you temporarily hide your profile when you need a dating-app break
- Plenty of prompts and profile features to help show off your personality
- SuperSwipes let you signal extra interest in a potential match
- Incognito Mode lets Premium and Premium+ members only be seen by people they’ve already liked
- Paid subscriptions offer perks like unlimited likes and advanced filters
- Travel Mode lets Premium and Premium+ members change their location before or during a trip
Cons:
- The 24-hour window to start a conversation can feel limiting if you don’t check the app regularly
- Some of the most useful features, including Incognito and Travel Mode, require a paid subscription
- Bumble’s conversation rules can take a minute to get used to if you’re coming from apps where anyone can immediately message a match
Price:
- Free to download and use
- Bumble Boost starts at around $14.99 per week
- Bumble Premium starts at around $27.99 per week
- Bumble Premium+ starts at around $39.99 per week
2. Hinge
Best For:
Daters who want to know more than someone’s height and favorite vacation spot before matching.
Why We Picked It:
The self-proclaimed “dating app designed to be deleted,” Hinge is an obvious contender if your ultimate goal is to get off dating apps altogether. “If you're searching for a dating platform that prioritizes depth over quick swipes, Hinge might be just what you're looking for,” says Mariah Freya, sex education expert and founder of Beducated. “It combines the best of Tinder's ease of use with Match's focus on genuine connections.”
Profiles include photos and videos, answers to prompts, and details like dating intentions and relationship type, giving you plenty to work with when deciding whether you might actually like someone. You can also like or comment on a specific part of someone’s profile rather than simply swiping on the whole person, and Hinge’s newer Convo Starters feature offers personalized suggestions based on a match’s profile when your brain simply cannot come up with another opening line.
Who It’s For:
Hinge is open to daters of all genders and orientations, but it’s particularly useful if you want more information about potential matches upfront and are looking for something beyond a hookup.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
Pros:
- Detailed profiles include photos, videos, voice, prompts, dating intentions, and relationship preferences
- You can like or comment on specific parts of someone’s profile, giving you a built-in conversation starter
- Convo Starters can help when you have absolutely no idea what to say
- Selfie Verification can help confirm that matches look like the person in their profile
- Hinge’s We Met feature asks about your dates after you exchange phone numbers with a match and uses that feedback to improve future recommendations
- Hinge+ offers unlimited likes and lets you see everyone who has liked you
- HingeX adds features like enhanced recommendations and Priority Likes
Cons:
- Free users have a limited number of likes
- Some of the features that make Hinge significantly easier to use are behind paid subscriptions
- Detailed profiles are great if you want depth, less great if filling out dating-app prompts is your personal hell
Price:
- Free to download and use
- Hinge+ starts at around $29.99 per month
- HingeX starts at around $49.99 per month
3. Tinder
Best For:
Having a ton of options.
Why We Picked It:
Tinder is basically the reason swiping became synonymous with dating apps in the first place, and its sheer size is still one of its biggest selling points. The app is available in more than 190 countries and has racked up more than 55 billion matches, so if your biggest dating problem is simply finding enough people to date, Tinder certainly gives you options. And while it has a reputation as a hookup app, you can specify what you’re looking for with Relationship Goals, including a long-term partner.
Who It’s For:
Tinder is open to daters of all genders and orientations and is a particularly good option if you want a large dating pool. Because people use Tinder for everything from casual hookups to serious relationships, though, pay attention to Relationship Goals and be upfront about what you’re looking for if long-term love is the goal.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
- Available on desktop via Tinder for Web
Pros:
- Huge dating pool with users around the world
- Easy to set up and start swiping
- Relationship Goals help you communicate what you’re looking for
- Photo Verification lets users verify that they look like their profile photos
- Rewind lets subscribers undo their last Like or Nope
- Passport Mode lets you change your location and match with people elsewhere
- Tinder Platinum includes Priority Likes, which helps your Likes and Super Likes get seen faster
Cons:
- A huge dating pool also means more profiles to wade through
- People use Tinder for all kinds of connections, so not everyone you encounter will be looking for a serious relationship
- Free users don’t get unlimited Likes
- Features like Rewind and Passport require a subscription or separate purchase
Price:
- Free to download and use
- Tinder Plus starts at around $9.99 per month
- Tinder Gold starts at around $13.99 per month
4. Hily
Best For:
Gen Z daters looking for a more intentional, inclusive dating experience.
Why We Picked It:
With a large Gen Z user base, Hily is clearly geared toward younger daters. The app has more than 43 million downloads and puts a big emphasis on authenticity, compatibility, and helping users find people who are actually looking for the same things they are.
One feature that especially stands out is Consent Guard, which is designed to help prevent unsolicited explicit messages and images. If the technology detects potentially sexual content, it prompts the sender to ask for consent before sending it, giving the recipient the option to accept or decline. Because nothing kills the possibility of a meaningful connection quite like an unsolicited nude from someone you exchanged three messages with.
Who It’s For:
Hily is especially suited to Gen Z daters who want to meet people based on more than a few carefully curated photos. It may also appeal to anyone who appreciates extra control over the kinds of sexual messages or images they receive while dating online.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
Pros:
- Particularly geared toward Gen Z and younger daters
- Consent Guard helps prevent unsolicited explicit messages and photos from reaching you without your consent
- Discover offers another way to find potential matches based on your interests and dating intentions
- Profile verification and other safety features help screen potential matches
- Compatibility features offer another way to evaluate potential matches beyond their photos
- You can add music to your profile, because music compatibility is very much a thing
Cons:
- Some features require a paid subscription
- May appeal less to older daters looking for a more traditional dating-app experience
Price:
- Free to download and use
- Hily Premium starts at around $14.99 per week
- Hily Premium+ starts at around $24.99 per week
- Additional in-app purchases, including profile boosts, are available
5. eharmony
Best For:
Daters who are serious about finding a long-term partner.
Why We Picked It:
eharmony has been around since 2000, which is approximately 400 years in dating-app time, but its focus on long-term compatibility is also what keeps it relevant for people who are serious about finding a relationship. Instead of immediately throwing you into an endless stack of profiles, the app has you complete a detailed Compatibility Quiz and uses your answers to generate matches and compatibility information.
“If you're ready to say ‘I do,’ then eharmony is there to guide you along the way,” Freya says. “Renowned for its emphasis on long-term commitment, it's like the Charlotte York of dating apps—traditional and mostly geared towards heterosexual relationships.” While you certainly don’t need to be ready for marriage tomorrow to use it, the more involved setup process and detailed profiles may appeal to daters who are willing to put a little more time into finding a compatible partner.
Who It’s For:
People looking for a serious, long-term relationship who don’t mind spending more time setting up their profile and answering compatibility questions upfront. It may also appeal to daters who prefer a more structured matching process over simply swiping through profiles.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
- Available on desktop
Pros:
- Detailed profiles and an in-depth Compatibility Quiz
- Compatibility information can help you evaluate potential matches
- Matching process is designed around long-term compatibility
- Particularly geared toward relationship-minded daters
- Free Basic membership lets you create a profile and browse matches
Cons:
- More time-consuming to set up than swipe-first apps
- Unlimited messaging and several other features require Premium
- Premium subscriptions require a longer commitment than many competing apps
- May feel a little traditional compared with newer dating apps
Price:
- Free Basic membership available
- Premium Light, typically a six-month commitment, runs roughly $59 to $69 per month
- Premium Plus, typically a 12-month commitment, runs roughly $38 to $50 per month
- Premium Extra, typically a 24-month commitment, runs roughly $29 to $33 per month
6. Match
Best For:
Serious daters who want a large, established dating pool.
Why We Picked It:
Match has been around since 1995, making it one of the OG online dating platforms—and there’s something to be said for an app that has survived approximately every era of internet dating. Unlike platforms that lean heavily into casual swiping, Match has long positioned itself toward people looking for relationships.
“Match is my top choice for its ability to cater to individuals in their 30s and 40s seeking meaningful connections,” Freya says. “Its large user base offers a wide range of like-minded adults looking for genuine relationships.” Profiles also give you plenty of space to spell out who you are and what you’re looking for, which can be especially useful when the goal is finding someone you might actually want to date long-term.
Who It’s For:
Relationship-minded daters who want a more traditional online dating experience and plenty of information about potential matches before deciding whether to connect.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
- Available on desktop
Pros:
- Large, established dating pool
- Detailed profiles let you learn more about potential matches upfront
- Geared toward people looking for relationships
- Search and filtering options can help narrow down potential matches
Cons:
- Many features require a paid subscription
- Can feel more traditional than newer dating apps
- Paid memberships can get pricey
- Longer subscriptions are generally billed upfront rather than month-to-month
Price:
- Free to join and use with limited features
- Standard plans run roughly $34.45 per month for three months, $24.48 per month for six months, or $21.84 per month for 12 months
- Premium plans run roughly $40.41 per month for three months, $26.51 per month for six months, or $23.11 per month for 12 months
- Multi-month plans are generally charged in full at the beginning of the subscription
7. OkCupid
Best For:
Daters who want to get specific about compatibility.
Why We Picked It:
OkCupid has been around since 2004, but it’s managed to evolve beyond its early-internet-dating roots. One of its biggest draws is the sheer number of questions you can answer about everything from relationships and lifestyle to politics, sex, and approximately whatever else you might want to know about someone before agreeing to spend two hours across a table from them.
Your answers help determine your compatibility with potential matches, and you can also specify what kind of relationship you’re looking for. That makes OkCupid especially useful if you have particular values, preferences, or dealbreakers you’d rather get out of the way sooner rather than later.
Who It’s For:
Daters who want a more inclusive app and like having plenty of information about potential matches upfront. It’s also a good option if you’d rather use compatibility questions to narrow down your dating pool than rely primarily on photos and a few prompts.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
- Available on desktop
Pros:
- Lots of compatibility questions to help you find people with similar values and preferences
- Inclusive gender and sexual-orientation options
- You can specify the type of relationship you’re looking for
- Free version offers plenty of functionality
- Available on desktop as well as mobile
Cons:
- Answering enough questions to get the most out of the compatibility features takes some time
- Some features and filters require a paid subscription
- The amount of information can feel like a lot if you prefer a simpler swipe-and-go experience
Price:
- Free to download and use
- OkCupid Premium starts at around $19.99 per month
- Additional paid features and Boosts are available
8. Flure
Best For:
Sex-positive daters looking for less traditional dating-app rules.
Why We Picked It:
A serious relationship doesn’t necessarily have to follow the traditional dating-app playbook, which is where Flure comes in. The app takes a more open-ended approach to dating, encouraging users to meet people and see where the connection goes rather than requiring them to define exactly what they’re looking for upfront. It also puts a particular emphasis on sex positivity, inclusivity, and creating a space where users can be open about what they want.
Flure also puts an emphasis on safety and communication. Its in-app features include Safe Mode, which helps protect users from unsolicited explicit content, and Flure Sparks, a game designed to help matches get to know each other and talk about everything from everyday interests to sex and relationships.
Who It’s For:
Sex-positive and open-minded daters who prefer a less rigid approach to defining what they’re looking for and want an app that leaves room for different kinds of connections.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS
Pros:
- Open-ended approach lets connections develop without requiring a relationship label upfront
- Flure Sparks offers built-in prompts to help matches get to know each other
- Safe Mode adds another layer of protection against unsolicited explicit content
- Welcoming to people looking for connections outside the traditional dating-app mold
Cons:
- Smaller dating pool than more established apps
- Its intentionally label-free approach may not appeal to daters who want to filter specifically for a long-term relationship from the start
Price:
- Free to download and use
- Premium costs around $29.99 per month
- Three-month subscriptions cost around $44.99
- Annual subscriptions cost around $107.99
9. BLK
Best For:
Black singles looking for meaningful connections.
Why We Picked It:
BLK is a dating and lifestyle app created specifically with the Black community in mind, giving Black singles a space to meet people without having to rely solely on the filters and preferences offered by more general dating apps. And if you’re looking for a serious relationship, being able to start with a dating pool centered around a shared cultural experience can make finding compatible matches a little easier.
The app also goes beyond one-on-one matching with BLK Community, which includes chat rooms organized around different interests and topics, giving users another way to connect beyond simply swiping through profiles.
Who It’s For:
Black singles looking to date, build relationships, and connect with other members of the Black community.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
Pros:
- Created specifically with Black singles in mind
- BLK Community offers chat rooms based on shared interests
- Super Likes let you signal extra interest in someone
- Rewind lets paid members go back if they accidentally pass on someone
- Paid tiers offer perks like unlimited likes, Boosts, and the ability to see who likes you
Cons:
- Smaller dating pool than major mainstream apps
- Some of the most useful features require a paid membership
Price:
- Free to download and use
- Premium starts at around $9.99 per week
- Elite starts at around $21.99 per week
- Platinum starts at around $29.99 per week or $49.99 per month
10. Plenty of Fish
Best For:
Daters who actually want to talk before meeting up.
Why We Picked It:
Plenty of Fish has been around since 2003, so it’s another dating app that predates swiping as we know it. But if you’re looking for something serious, its emphasis on conversation can be a plus. Rather than making every interaction feel like a split-second decision based on a few photos, POF gives users plenty of ways to actually talk and get to know potential matches.
The app also has an “Are You Sure?” feature designed to detect potentially inappropriate language and give you a chance to reconsider a message before sending it. Because sometimes the difference between a promising match and an immediate unmatch is simply taking two seconds to reread what you typed.
Who It’s For:
Daters who prefer getting to know someone through conversation and want an app that feels a little less focused on endlessly swiping through profiles.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
- Available on desktop
Pros:
- Conversation-focused features make it easier to get to know matches
- “Are You Sure?” encourages users to reconsider potentially inappropriate messages before sending
- Search features let you get more specific about what you’re looking for
- Large, established dating platform
- Free version lets you access many of the app’s core features
Cons:
- Interface may feel a little dated compared with newer dating apps
- Some features require a paid membership
Price:
- Free to download and use
- POF Premium starts at around $29.99 per month
- One-week subscriptions are available for around $19.99
- Additional Tokens and other in-app purchases are available
11. Happn
Best For:
Meeting someone you might actually cross paths with IRL.
Why We Picked It:
If you’d ideally like to date someone who lives in your general vicinity, Happn puts a digital spin on the old-school meet-cute. The location-based app helps you discover people you’ve crossed paths with IRL, whether that’s someone who frequents the same coffee shop, lives in your neighborhood, or apparently has the exact same Target schedule you do.
For daters looking for something serious, there’s an obvious practical upside: Your matches are already spending time in the same places you are. And while Happn can’t guarantee you’ll end up in a rom-com-worthy meet-cute, it can make meeting someone nearby a little easier than waiting to dramatically bump into a hot stranger on the sidewalk.
Who It’s For:
Daters who want to meet people nearby and like the idea of connecting with someone they may already cross paths with in their everyday life.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
- Available on desktop via the Happn web app
Pros:
- Location-based matching helps you find people you’ve crossed paths with
- Particularly useful if dating someone nearby is important to you
- You can use Happn on desktop via its web app
- Boost can increase your profile’s visibility
- Offers a more IRL-inspired approach to discovering potential matches
Cons:
- Smaller dating pool than some of the biggest dating apps
- Less useful in areas where there aren’t many active users
- Location-based matching means you may encounter some of the same profiles repeatedly
- Not ideal if you’re primarily interested in meeting people outside your area
Price:
- Free to download and use
- Happn Premium subscriptions are available
- Boosts and other in-app purchases are also available
12. HER
Best For:
Queer women, lesbians, and nonbinary daters.
Why We Picked It:
HER bills itself as “the sapphic dating app,” and unlike mainstream dating apps that simply offer LGBTQ+ identity and preference settings, the platform was built specifically around queer dating and community. That can make a pretty major difference when you’re looking for a serious relationship and would rather not spend half your time figuring out whether someone is actually available to date you.
“HER isn't your average dating app—it's a vibrant community and dating platform designed specifically for queer women and non-binary individuals,” Freya says. “If you've ever felt out of place or uncomfortable on mainstream apps, HER offers a safe haven. It's a welcoming space where you can truly be yourself and connect with like-minded queer folks who understand your experiences.”
Who It’s For:
Lesbian, bisexual, queer, and other sapphic women, as well as nonbinary and trans daters who identify with the community HER serves.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
Pros:
- Built specifically for sapphic and queer dating
- Offers community features in addition to one-on-one matching
- Helps users discover queer events and gatherings
- Gives users plenty of gender identity and sexuality options
- Free version includes core matching, messaging, events, and community features
Cons:
- Not designed for straight daters or cisgender men
- Some filters and additional features require a paid subscription
- Unlimited swiping requires a paid membership
Price:
- Free to download and use
- HER Premium starts at around $14.99 per month
13. EliteSingles
Best For:
Career-minded daters looking for something serious.
Why We Picked It:
If career, education, and ambition are high on your list of things you’d like to have in common with a partner, EliteSingles is built around helping you find people with similar priorities. The app is geared specifically toward relationship-minded singles and uses a personality questionnaire and your dating preferences to recommend compatible matches.
“If you're a go-getter in both your career and personal life and find the usual dating apps a bit uninspiring, EliteSingles might be just what you need,” Freya says. “It's like the exclusive club of dating apps—perfect for ambitious, successful individuals seeking genuine connections. While the membership fee may be higher, it serves as a barrier, ensuring you meet people who are as serious about finding a partner as you are.”
Who It’s For:
Daters who are looking for a long-term relationship and particularly interested in meeting other career- and education-minded singles.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
- Available on desktop
Pros:
- Geared specifically toward people looking for serious relationships
- Personality questionnaire helps inform your match recommendations
- Particularly focused on career- and education-minded singles
- Detailed profiles give you more information about potential matches upfront
Cons:
- Free membership is fairly limited
- Smaller dating pool than major mainstream apps
- Premium membership can be expensive
- Not ideal if you prefer browsing a huge pool of matches on your own
Price:
- Free Basic membership available with limited features
- Premium costs around $64.99 for one month
- Three-month Premium membership costs around $34.99 per month
- Six-month Premium membership costs around $28.33 per month
- Multi-month subscriptions are charged upfront
14. Beyond
Best For:
Polyamorous and ethically non-monogamous daters.
Why We Picked It:
Looking for a serious relationship doesn’t necessarily mean looking for a monogamous one. Beyond is an inclusive, members-only dating app that lets users specify and filter by relationship style as well as sexual orientation, making it particularly useful for polyamorous and ethically non-monogamous daters who want to be upfront about what they’re looking for.
“I’d suggest Beyond because it has more of a social element that most apps are missing,” King says. “Beyond’s core mission is to ‘curate a community for honest and intentional dating.’ Because of its mission, the founders host consistent in-person meetups for users in various cities in the U.S., which creates a more organic dating experience that naturally leads to creating a solid connection.”
Who It’s For:
Sex-positive and community-minded daters, particularly those who are polyamorous, ethically non-monogamous, or looking for other nontraditional relationship structures.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS
Pros:
- Lets you filter by dating preference, including monogamous, monogamish, open, polyamorous, exploring, and looking for friends
- Lets you filter by sexuality, gender, and relationship status
- Hosts IRL events and meetups in select cities
- Members go through an application process before joining
- Community-focused approach offers ways to connect beyond traditional swiping
Cons:
- Currently only available on iOS
- IRL events aren’t available everywhere
- Membership approval can take some time
- Smaller dating pool than mainstream apps
- May not be the best fit if you’re specifically looking for a traditional monogamous relationship
Price:
- Free to download
- Weekly memberships start at around $14.99
- Monthly memberships start at around $19.99
- Three-month memberships cost around $74.99
- Additional purchases, including Direct Requests and Skip the Wait, are available
15. The League
Best For:
Career-focused daters looking for an equally ambitious partner.
Why We Picked It:
If your career is a major part of your life and you’d like to date someone who gets that, The League is built specifically around connecting ambitious, career-minded singles. Unlike apps where you can download and immediately start swiping, The League has an application process and may place prospective members on a waitlist before they’re admitted.
That extra barrier to entry won’t be for everyone, but if you’re looking for a serious relationship with someone who has similar professional priorities, the more curated dating pool may be part of the appeal.
Who It’s For:
Career-focused singles who want to meet other ambitious daters and don’t mind a more selective application process.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS
Pros:
- Geared toward ambitious, career-focused daters
- Application process creates a more curated dating pool
- Offers a curated daily batch of potential matches rather than an endless stream of profiles
- Particularly useful if career compatibility matters to you in a long-term partner
Cons:

item.source: ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
item.dc:creator: Clare Armstrong
item.description: In short: Almost all women surveyed in a new Australian study reported encountering harmful behaviour on dating apps, with many taking their own precautions to stay safe. Researchers say platforms should do more to prevent systemic risks as the federal government considers a digital duty of care. What's next? item.content:encoded:
In short:
Almost all women surveyed in a new Australian study reported encountering harmful behaviour on dating apps, with many taking their own precautions to stay safe.
Researchers say platforms should do more to prevent systemic risks as the federal government considers a digital duty of care.
What's next?
Consultation on Labor's proposed digital duty of care closes on Tuesday, with advocates saying it has capacity to curb online abuse.
Women are being forced to act as their own safety system on dating apps where experiences of sexual harassment, manipulation and controlling behaviours are widespread, a study has found.
Australian researchers found 99 per cent of heterosexual women surveyed had encountered at least one harmful behaviour on a dating app in the previous three months.
Unsolicited explicit messages, attempts to monitor activity, love bombing, negging and gaslighting are common experiences on dating apps, according to the study released on Tuesday by the Minderoo Foundation-funded Behaviour Insights Team (BIT).
Women reported routinely screening profiles for warning signs, withholding identifying information and carefully managing interactions to protect themselves from potential harm.
These accounts have fuelled calls to ensure a proposed digital duty of care was implemented to require online services to tackle systemic risks.
Researchers have argued the scale of the problem showed women could not be expected to manage the risks alone, with dating platforms better placed to prevent harm before it occurred.
Women coaching each other to stay safe
Brisbane resident Rebecca Wilson, 33, said her harmful dating app experiences have included receiving "completely unsolicited" and "aggressively sexual" messages, photos and videos.
Ms Wilson said she was also once stalked by a man she had met via an app.
"We went on one date. I said to him, 'Look I'm just not interested anymore', and he didn't get the message," she said.
"Weeks later he kept popping up at the same places as me … following me around.
"He touched me at a bar right in front of my friends when it was clearly unsolicited."
With only minimal information on the man, Ms Wilson said she could not easily report him to authorities.
One issue was that using the "block" feature on the app meant she lost the ability to collect identifying material to progress a complaint.
"There's no way of being able to know the identity of who you were talking to," Ms WIlson said.
Ms Wilson said she and her friends have "coached" each other through how to navigate online dating safely.
"The current mechanisms are really just not enough on these apps," she said.
Harmful behaviour 'normalised'
The most common harmful behaviours on dating apps were psychological and emotional, which were encountered by 95 per cent of the 1,008 women across Australia surveyed for the BIT study.
About 89 per cent experienced monitoring and surveillance activity and 88 per cent reported being sent unsolicited sexual images and videos, and being pressured and manipulated into sending sexual content.
Almost six in 10 women reported fear-based controlling behaviour, including threats of physical harm. Of those, only about 22 per cent reported those threats to the platforms.
Among women who made reports to platforms generally, about 19 per cent felt their complaint was "barely" or "not at all" taken seriously, while 64 per cent said they were taken at least "somewhat" seriously.
Lead researcher Karen Tindall said the findings showed there was a need for greater efforts by the platforms to tackle "genuinely preventable risk".
"Right now, a lot of these behaviours are so normalised that women blame themselves or they think they are overreacting," she said.
"This data and research should validate women's experience and should shift the conversation toward fixing the system itself."
Dr Tindall said there were features built for safety that could lead to harm, such as preventing screenshots to prevent against image-based abuse.
"But that also removes a woman's ability to document what happened," she said.
"I'm not saying those safety features should be removed, but it means that safety features need to be tested for how they will be worked around, and whether they will work as intended."
Duty would shift responsibility onto platforms
The findings have been released as the federal government consults on its proposed digital duty of care, which is intended to require services to identify and mitigate foreseeable risks rather than relying on users to report harm after the fact.
The draft duty for adults could apply to dating platforms on which users have faced serious abuse, stalking, sexual violence or image-based abuse.
It would mean services were required to identify and mitigate systemic risks that could enable such conduct.
While the initial debate has focused on social media, the proposed duty would apply more broadly across digital services, including dating and messaging apps, online games, search engines and AI services.
Minderoo Foundation gender equality executive director Jacqueline Joudo Larsen said a digital duty of care could prevent harm and protect Australians.
"It is the single biggest lever to curb the reach, scale and speed at which abuse is occurring by shifting responsibility from individuals to companies that are designing and operating online platforms," she said.
"This is a standard that we hold other sectors to and it should be no different for the online space."
Ms Larsen said technology had "transformed" how people met, connected and built relationships.
"Those benefits are very meaningful," she said.
"But safety cannot be the price women pay for participation.
"This is a design problem that's entirely preventable."
Ms Larsen said Australia could be a leader in tech safety and, if it was serious about ending sexual and domestic violence, that was an "opportunity we can't squander".
Labor's proposal under scrutiny
Submissions on Labor's proposal close on Tuesday and draft legislation will likely be introduced next month.
The Coalition has criticised the draft, primarily due to concerns over discretionary powers allowing the minister to add additional "harms" for children and "serious harms" for adults.
In a social media post shared by Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, the Coalition dubbed the idea the "Albo-rithm" and suggested the government would seek to censor online spaces.
But Communications Minister Anika Wells has repeatedly said the intent of the rule making power was about acting with "urgency" if new threats, such as apps that allowed users to "nudify" photos, arose online.
"We think this is a sensible measure to try and deal with these emerging harms that are coming online every single day," she said earlier this month.
The discretion in the bill for adding additional harms would be disallowable by the Senate at any time, but Labor might have to make some changes to their plan in order to secure the Greens' support for the draft bill.
In another submission to the draft legislation, the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman has described the reforms as a "rare opportunity" to build trust and accountability into the digital economy from the outset.
Ombudsman Cynthia Gebert said trust would not be built by hoping companies did the right thing and urged the government to consider an independent external dispute mechanism for when system failures occurred.
"Everyday Australians need someone to turn to for support holding big tech companies accountable when they get things wrong and we stand ready to help," she said.
The submission said an external complaints system would provide a "practical avenue" for Australians to resolve issues such as restoration of account access, ensuring choices about algorithms are implemented and reconsidering incorrect decisions.

item.content:encoded:
After years of captivating users with endless swipes, dating apps are now trying to get people to put their phones down and find connection in the real world.
Tinder, the pioneer of the dating swipe, is now one of the companies leading this expansion of IRL events. In March, the company introduced an Events feature in its app and hosted a pilot event for users in Los Angeles.
Since then, the feature has started to catch on, especially with younger people, said Tinder chief product officer Mark Kantor. The company since March has seen 71% of its Gen Z users in L.A. visit the Events feature on its app. Meanwhile, only 63% of users 25 and older engaged with it.
The company has now expanded the feature to 20 cities, mostly in the U.S. but also in Europe. The idea, Kantor told Fortune via email, is to shed the label of “dating event” and instead allow users to meet potential matches while doing something they already love like pickleball, trivia, or sauna and cold plunge sessions.
The company has partnered with several companies to facilitate these kinds of activities including City Pickle, Joust, and Othership.
“The activity gives people a natural starting point, and the shared experience takes some of the pressure out of meeting someone new,” he said.
Another established dating app company, Bumble, said it is also helping extend its reach beyond swipes and messages with events and activations. This year, the company has taken over bars across New York for singles mixers, hosted a rooftop party in Nashville, and held an event with Barstool Sports’ Tommy Smokes in Boston.
“IRL has been part of Bumble’s DNA from the start. We know that one of the biggest points of friction in dating today is the gap between connecting online and actually meeting in person, and we’re focused on helping close that gap,” a Bumble spokesperson told Fortune in a statement.
Outside of dating apps, Gen Z and other young people have increasingly turned to in-person activities like run clubs for a sense of community, and also for romantic connection. According to Strava, participation in run clubs grew 59% over the past two years. At the same time, Gen Z is drinking less alcohol at bars and clubs, to the dismay of the night life industry.
Dating app companies’ increasing push for real-world events comes as user numbers have fallen.
Tinder’s daily active users were down 4% year over year in the second quarter, which was a slight improvement compared to past quarters. Paying Tinder users fell to 8.5 million as of the second quarter, an 11.5% drop compared to the same period two years earlier.
Bumble has experienced a steeper decline, with total paying users falling to 3.2 million in the second quarter from 4.1 million two years earlier—a 24% drop.
Swipe fatigue
Partly to blame for these declines may be swipe fatigue. A study of nearly 9,000 respondents from reverse lookup company Clarity Check in July found that 58% of respondents had deleted a dating app because they found it “emotionally draining.” Another 44% said they would prefer to meet someone in a low-pressure setting rather than get to know them through a profile.
Breeze, a dating app based in Delft, Netherlands, was created explicitly to get people to meet rather than swipe. The company, which has a team of 41 and has raised about $7 million in funding, charges by date rather than subscription.
Each user receives only a handful of profiles each day. If two people match, they fill out their availability rather than opening a chat, and then Breeze brings the pair together at a partner venue.
“A short real-world date tells you more about compatibility than weeks of texting, and it does it faster and with less of the anxiety and second-guessing that endless chat creates,” Marco van der Woude, Breeze’s cofounder and head of business development, told Fortune in an email.

item.content:encoded:
Dating apps were already hard enough.
Now imagine spending weeks flirting with someone, buying virtual coins just to keep talking to them and maybe even getting emotionally attached…
only to discover your situationship was basically ChatGPT with a profile picture.
Security researchers have uncovered a surprisingly sophisticated network of dating apps using AI-generated personas to convince users they were talking to real people.
Apps including Dora, Romi and Doni reportedly used thousands of fake personas capable of chatting around the clock, sending messages and keeping users engaged , while the apps encouraged them to spend money on virtual currency to continue conversations.
And this wasn’t some tiny operation.
Researchers identified more than 4,700 AI personas, interacting with around 25,000 users and sending 2.36 million messages in just two weeks.
The whole thing was apparently built like an actual tech company, with growth plans, payment systems and tools designed to help the apps pass app-store reviews.
So yes.
Catfishing has officially received a software update.
At this point, before falling in love online, apparently we also need to ask:
“Select all the traffic lights in this picture.”

item.content:encoded:
Dating apps are in a weird place right now.
Culturally, people are starting to hate them. Whether out of personal distaste or for safety and privacy, more people want to return to the real world to find connections. But dating apps are still big business. Match Group reported net income of $613.5 million in 2025, up from $551.3 million in 2024 but down from $651.5 million in 2023. (Match Group owns Tinder, Hinge, and a slew of other dating apps.) So, despite the complaints, they're still making money, and a lot of it.
And the ecosystem is getting increasingly niche. There's an app for conservatives. For leftists. Farmers. Christians. Christian Farmers. The rich. The famous. People who like movies. Double daters. Freaks who use 4chan. And now, entering the field as of last week, the dating app for people who read.
You May Also Like
AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections
Tinder — top pick for finding hookups
Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups
Hearing that a dating app for readers now exists is, at this point, not novel. But what piqued my interest is that the app was being developed by Co-Star, the astrology app. Now that's novel. Beyond that, with the backing of the Co-Star brand and ecosystem, it commands interest among young adults who like astrology and are considered popular and fashionable, i.e., socialite New Yorkers and Brooklyn-based culture writers.
Readme is a book reader's dating app, and its mission is to match people spiritually, much like the classic "meet cute" at the bookstore. And maybe, just maybe, spark relationships where they don't have to expose their (male) partners for being illiterate.
It's a book-series-sized task from the Co-Star creators. However, from my brief experience with the app, I found it to be ambitious but not well-crafted enough to justify waiting for the next installment.
Getting started with Readme
Setting up an account is no different than any other app.
Users fill out their name, age, gender, dating preference, and what they're looking for. One of the app's two big hooks is that your queue of potential matches is built or can be filtered around your friends and people that are associated within two or three degrees of them. Kinda like old-school Hinge or Tinder's short-lived Friends of Friends feature.
Within the app, one of the filters lets you see only your friends, your friends' friends, or your friends' friends' friends. It's interesting in theory, in that Readme wants to replicate those meet-cute type moments that you read about in books. Not in practice, though, because none of my friends are on the app or know it exists. It just launched, after all. But maybe this is my sign to start hosting more parties.
The other big hook is the quiz that "uses psycholinguistics to explore the hidden links between how you read and how you relate," according to the app. It's 25 questions, with the bulk asking you to pick which of two quotes you like or dislike the least. After you pick, it reveals which author it was.
For example, some of the authors I got were Henry Miller, Robert Frost, Casey McQuiston (of Red, White, & Royal Blue fame), and Jonathan Safran Foer. The latter was personally embarassing cause I really, really dislike Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close, as a book and a movie.
Between the quotes are questions about your political beliefs, communication style, and the genres of books you like to read. The latter was particularly irritating because much of the copy in the app has millennial-esque snark that tries to be "smashpunk" but is just grating. I like reading historical non-fiction, and the closest option to that was "straight up facts." Another genre option was "the writing on the wall," which is so eye-rolling. Obviously, these are my own personal misgivings, but Readme somehow tries too hard not to be like the other apps, yet also wants you to know it's cool, hip, and too irony-pilled to be authentic.
At the end of the day, language like that is fine, but seeing "communism will win" and "nostalgic for Barack Obama" as options under "political beliefs" did get a laugh out of me.
Something not included in the questionnaire, or seemingly anywhere on Readme, is astrological signs. Nowhere to put my birthdate, time, and place. So if you're looking for astrological compatability, Readme isn't it. (Yet?)
After the questionnaire, you get a report on what your language preferences "reveal about who you are and how you love."
I got "Former Gifted Child" because I prefer metonymy over metaphor. The app's way of telling me I lack imagination. "You rely on structures and systems to make sense of the world," the app tells me. I wouldn't say it's wrong, because my parents always believed I was a precocious kid. Turns out I had ADHD the whole time, so maybe the app was onto something.
The report also details How I Love and What You Need. Overall, the report is neat but a bit basic if you remove the flowery language. I like the book recommendations it gave me, and it even gave me some questions I should ask on a first date. Per my ReadMe report, I'm a lover boy at heart and need someone who's not as rigid.
"You need someone who finds the social script so uninteresting that they haven't bothered reading it, and don't know or care whether they're following or breaking it," my report read. Sometimes it's hard to tell whether the copy was written by a millennial ad executive or by ChatGPT's poor interpretation of one.
Using the Readme app
So now that the setup is done, what's the actual app like? It's....fine. It's definitely a dating app. You click the heart to like and the minus sign to dislike. At the bottom of every profile, you'll see a similarity score based on their quiz answers and choices. And that's it, honestly.
The big glaring issue here is that Readme just doesn't have the juice yet.
Immediately upon getting to the app proper, my recommended likes all live in New York. I live in Chicago. There's no filter or setting for distance. The only settings you can change are age, gender, and mutuals. For me, the app is a nonstarter. Not that it can't be successful, but I live in the third-largest city in the U.S., and Readme's algorithm is only showing me people who don't live in my city. Maybe it should've had a limited launch in Brooklyn first, gotten some hype, and then rolled out to other major cities.
I swiped right on between 70 and 80 profiles in my selected age range (24-32) before running out of people to see. None of them was based in Chicago. I saw accounts from Vermont, New Jersey, Denver, San Francisco, and even Tokyo. But not one in 70+ swipes lived in Chicago or set their location as Chicago.
I guess on the positive side, unlike the big power players like Hinge and Tinder, you do have unlimited likes. It'll be interesting to see if that'll be the case as the app gets more attention — venture capital and vibes can only subsidize an app for so long. Maybe then the dating pool will keep me invested enough not to be on the app when the bill comes due.
To be frank, having a cis hetero male perspective on the dating app for readers probably doesn't give one a sense of what the dating pool is like. Statistically, people don't read that much in general, but women read far more often than men. According to a Pew Research Center study conducted in Oct. 2025, "women are more likely than men to say they've read a book in the past 12 months."
One can extrapolate from the many cultural reasons why women read more than men. I imagine the main appeal of an app like Readme for women is that avid reading can be seen as a sign of intelligence, empathy, and curiosity. With the rise of dudebro, Barstool conservatism in young men, an online dating app that, to an extent, filters one from an embarrassing partner, is appealing.
All of that said, this is from my perspective as a 28-year-old Black man living in Chicago. The aesthetic leanings of Readme's dating pool are what you'd expect from an app that markets itself as a zine-style, indie sleaze, Y2K vintage fashion store you'd find in the more affluent parts of Brooklyn. In short, it's very white. Which is not bad, and I don't mean to imply that there aren't women of color on the app, but as it's been researched before, dating apps' algorithms are not kind to Black women, or people of color in general.
It's a shame because its style and interface are easy to get acclimated with, but beyond the mutuals feature and the quiz, it doesn't really do enough to stand out. If anything, what sets Readme apart from the crowd of hyper-niche dating apps is that it knows and markets itself exactly towards the audience it wants.
That's fine, but it'd be interesting to see whether it can expand beyond that — if it even wants to.
Chance Townsend is the General Assignments Editor at Mashable, covering tech, video games, dating apps, digital culture, and whatever else comes his way. He has a Master's in Journalism from the University of North Texas and is a proud orange cat father. His writing has also appeared in PC Mag and Mother Jones.
In his free time, he cooks, loves to sleep, and greatly enjoys Detroit sports. If you have any tips or want to talk shop about the Lions, you can reach out to him on Bluesky @offbrandchance.bsky.social, by email at [email protected], or on Signal at 224-417-6628.

item.content:encoded:
Claire-Louise Bennett has said she is fascinated by the ways we exist in other people’s minds, by what we become when we are reduced to an idea. Perhaps that is why her fiction is always filtered through a consciousness: someone obsessively searching for a way out, or for a place in the world. Is love a kind of compass? Can it give shape to the self, each time in a different way?
Bennett thinks it should, but she also believes we are increasingly preventing it from doing so. Dating apps are no help, she says. In her latest novel, the intense, labyrinthine and deeply interior Big Kiss, Bye-Bye, she asks how love places us before a mirror and reveals the parts of ourselves we would never admit are also there. And something like that can only be reached, as Anaïs Nin might have put it, through the mystery of what draws us to another person when nothing has been agreed in advance.
At her home in Galway, Ireland, Bennett, who is also the author of Checkout 19 and Pond, answers the video call. She is seated at an enormous table. It is covered with notebooks and crystal spheres. Nearby, she says, there is even a glass penguin. And the mug from which she occasionally takes a sip still contains some of the Yogi Choco tea she made for herself a little while ago.
Question. Big Kiss, Bye-Bye is a long conversation between two lovers that recalls both the obsessive prose of Thomas Bernhard and the stream of consciousness of Virginia Woolf. In that conversation, Xavier functions as a kind of totem, a looming presence against which the narrator defines herself, sketching an outline of who she is and making herself real. To what extent is love a kind of existential compass?
Answer. I love the image. Yes. Without a doubt, it is. I deeply believe that love is an existential experience. I read Alain Badiou’s In Praise of Love a long time ago and felt he was right about everything. At the center of the experience of love should be difference, chance and risk — elements that today, in a world dominated by app-mediated dating, are practically impossible. Today’s world encourages us to think in terms of compatibility. We look for someone who fits us, who reaffirms who we already are. That very conscious way of approaching relationships can be quite transactional, like shopping, because it forces us to define in advance what we are looking for in a partner, what we expect from a relationship and what our limits are. Love is the opposite. Love is the great revealer.
Q. In what sense?
A. Love reveals who we really are. It shows us things about ourselves we would never have dared to imagine, much less admit. That is why attraction that arises in real life has such enormous force and, at the same time, is so unsettling. Anaïs Nin was terrified of being fixed into a stable, defined personality. She wanted to flow, to be always transforming, and for her love, made that perpetual motion possible — that existential expansion. Her stories and novels show how intimate encounters can uproot you, turn your world upside down, take you far from whoever you think you are at that moment. What today might be dismissed as mere romanticism is, in reality, what makes love a deeply singular experience. After all, it is the most powerful force there is, provided one has the courage not to try to manage or direct it.
Q. In your case, writing itself also seems to function as a compass, a way of finding your path through words and through what words construct: fragmentary scenes, memories seen from a single perspective, disorientation, something mutable and therefore open to transformation. Would you say that’s true? What are we, really? Everything we might yet become, or everything we have been?
A. Sometimes I feel I do not have a self, at least not in a strict sense. What I am is a place where very diverse forces orbit — and sometimes conflict —: archetypes, psychic patterns, impulses and memories both personal and collective, and many other things. There is a huge part of what I am that is completely unknown to me. And yet I know those unknown elements exert a huge influence on my everyday life. It is tempting to use writing as a way to make sense of that chaos and learn to navigate it, but the satisfaction it offers is only superficial. That is not what I am looking for. Samuel Beckett said the artist’s task is not to clarify things, but to find a way to make room for disorder. I completely agree.
Q. Is that why your writing has this quality of being unreliable, of constantly transforming itself?
A. Yes. My writing follows a winding path, full of false starts, dead ends, and overgrown landscapes. And, every now and then, small clearings appear where there is a sense of respite, immediacy, and communion. The thing is, I don’t write to affirm anything. I write by denying, subverting, and undermining. And that’s because, although we need to place some faith in reality in order to keep on living, deep down I don’t believe that what we call reality actually exists.

item.content:encoded:
You won’t see a more concentrated instance of how funny and frustrating Ted Lasso can be at the same time than an overly long bit where Ted fills out his dating profile. In signature Lasso fashion, mundane questions are but prompts for Ted to run wild with his brand of mistaken yet sincere and wholesome wit. (And what a way to target me, personally, with references to Stephen Sondheim’s Company and David Fincher’s Zodiac.) It’s cute, mostly, until it gets embarrassing. I fail to find a more apt summary for Ted Lasso as a whole.
In the seventh episode of season 4, “Yes & Baby,” we finally take a closer look into the lives of the Lady Greyhounds. It’s a safe assumption that playing second division women’s football doesn’t match up to Premier League paydays, but the series makes a legitimate effort to show what, exactly, all the women have to lose if they don’t shape up and get butts into stadium seats fast enough. Meanwhile, Rebecca and the Richmond front office navigate the uglier sides of the football business as Dani Rojas’s scummy agent tries some underhanded negotiating. Coach Alice (Tanya Reynolds), now in the new year, learns the power of “yes,” while Roy Kent’s love life hits a serious juncture.
Then, there’s Ted. He has permission to date now, which he always had and didn’t need, but it’s meaningful to have the door open for him. But it’s been a while since Ted put himself out there. And have you heard? Dating sucks now. Sucks! Vox’s Today, Explained just did a whole episode about it. Ted’s walking back into the jungles after a lifetime of domesticity, and he’s frozen stiff by a questionnaire.
I don’t blame him. Imagine being Ted, a grown man on the other side of a decade-plus-long marriage with a kid in high school. Being asked to describe oneself in three words must be banal, mortifying, and not the least bit embarrassing. Which is why I appreciate the resolution the episode offers to Ted, and perhaps all of us in the trenches of apps and endless first dates. Before we can commit ourselves to someone else, it’s critical that we recognize our own worth and love ourselves first.
What a beautiful sentiment. If only the rest of Ted Lasso were as brilliant and graceful.
“Yes & Baby” is hardly a stinker—I’d even wager to say it’s a rather good episode—but it’s just another episode where Ted Lasso’s forward progress feels perpetually hindered by its umpteenth step on a rake. I was on board for so much of it. Really. Rebecca, Zelda, and Leslie’s cartoonish phone call had me in stitches (I need Zelda’s “KAHK-sacker” as a text alert), and the farewell between Roy and Dr. Beaumont (Laura Haddock) was genuinely moving. The latter reminded me how, after watching an early cut of Spider-Man 2, Chris Carrabba of Dashboard Confessional wrote “Vindicated,” a song centered on the significance of recognizing someone else. (“I am seeing in me now the things you swore you saw yourself.”) How apt the song plays in the end credits after Peter and MJ decide on a life together, no secrets or masks between them. No, Roy and Dr. Erin don’t capital-L love each other in the same way, but there’s genuine power still in telling someone that you see them.
I’m not even mad at the convenient resolution over the “Believe” sign subplot either. When the team sees Coach Alice taping Ted’s new sign in their locker room, they’re swift to a deep and callous cynicism that even Ted Lasso’s folksy superpowers seem powerless to fix. But all it takes is Lizzie’s adorable four-year-old to read it aloud and they’re suddenly motivated to, well, “believe.” (And win.) Their transformation comes from nowhere and it’s all very tonally maudlin—which is, let’s be real here, typical Ted Lasso—but it’s got enough of the show’s missing season 1 magic to sweep me away.
Which is why I am irritated that the show habitually resorts to eye-rolling zingers and punchlines. The whole two-minute stretch where Keeley helps Ted fill his profile runs the gamut of cringe to funny to embarrassing to impressive to cringe again. (And to not even play The Greatest American Hero theme over the end credits? Come on! Whack!)
I like fun and whimsy too. And I can appreciate Jason Sudeikis’s karaoke pipes. But having your middle-aged protagonist swear he’s “invited to the cookout” and is pro-pronouns... Man, it’s just exhausting for what is ultimately just a ninety-second gag. Nothing about this sinks Ted Lasso completely. But it’s discouraging how the show can be capable of wisdom and grace only to zap the air out of the room with weak grasps for—I’ll say it, I don’t care—woke points. At the end of the episode, Ted himself finds the three words to describe himself: “I am lovable.” That’s beautiful. That works. It’s amazing how little can go a long way.
